In sooth I know not why I am so sad, / It wearies me, you say it wearies you; / But how I caught it, found it, or came by it, / What stuff 'tis made of, whereof it is born, / I am to learn. / And such a want-wit sadness makes of me, / That I have much ado to know myself.

Honestly, I don't know why I'm so sad. It wears me out, and you say it wears you out too. But how I caught it, found it or came by it, what it's made of and where it comes from, I have yet to learn. And this sadness makes me so witless that I can hardly recognise myself.

Your mind is tossing on the ocean, / There where your argosies, with portly sail / Like signiors and rich burghers on the flood, / Or as it were the pageants of the sea, / Do overpeer the petty traffickers / That curtsy to them, do them reverence, / As they fly by them with their woven wings.

Your mind is tossing about out on the ocean, where your great merchant ships, with their billowing sails, sail like lords and rich citizens on the waves, or like floats in a pageant at sea. They look down on the little trading boats, which bob and bow to them as they fly past on their woven sails.

Believe me, sir, had I such venture forth, / The better part of my affections would / Be with my hopes abroad. I should be still / Plucking the grass to know where sits the wind, / Peering in maps for ports, and piers and roads; / And every object that might make me fear / Misfortune to my ventures, out of doubt / Would make me sad.

Believe me, sir, if I had such a venture at sea, most of my feelings would be out there with my hopes. I'd keep pulling up blades of grass to see which way the wind was blowing, and poring over maps for ports, piers and harbours. Anything that made me afraid of some disaster to my cargo would certainly make me sad.

My wind cooling my broth / Would blow me to an ague when I thought / What harm a wind too great might do at sea. / I should not see the sandy hour-glass run / But I should think of shallows and of flats, / And see my wealthy Andrew dock'd in sand, / Vailing her high top lower than her ribs / To kiss her burial. Should I go to church / And see the holy edifice of stone / And not bethink me straight of dangerous rocks, / Which, touching but my gentle vessel's side, / Would scatter all her spices on the stream, / Enrobe the roaring waters with my silks, / And, in a word, but even now worth this, / And now worth nothing? Shall I have the thought / To think on this, and shall I lack the thought / That such a thing bechanc'd would make me sad? / But tell not me, I know Antonio / Is sad to think upon his merchandise.

My own breath, cooling my soup, would give me a fever when I thought what harm too strong a wind could do at sea. I couldn't watch the sand run through an hourglass without thinking of sandbanks and shallows, and picturing my rich ship stuck fast in sand, her tall mast bowed lower than her hull, kissing her own grave. If I went to church and saw the holy stone building, wouldn't I think at once of dangerous rocks, which would only have to touch my fine ship's side to scatter all her spices on the water and wrap the roaring waves in my silks? In a word, worth this much one minute and nothing the next? Could I think about all this and not realise that if it happened it would make me sad? Don't tell me otherwise. I know Antonio is sad because he's thinking about his merchandise.

Believe me, no. I thank my fortune for it, / My ventures are not in one bottom trusted, / Nor to one place; nor is my whole estate / Upon the fortune of this present year. / Therefore my merchandise makes me not sad.
Believe me, no. Thank my luck, I haven't trusted all my goods to one ship, or to one place, and my whole fortune doesn't depend on how this one year goes. So my merchandise isn't what makes me sad.
Why then you are in love.

Not in love neither? Then let us say you are sad / Because you are not merry; and 'twere as easy / For you to laugh and leap and say you are merry / Because you are not sad. Now, by two-headed Janus, / Nature hath fram'd strange fellows in her time: / Some that will evermore peep through their eyes, / And laugh like parrots at a bagpiper. / And other of such vinegar aspect / That they'll not show their teeth in way of smile / Though Nestor swear the jest be laughable.

Not in love either? Then let's say you're sad because you're not happy. It would be just as easy for you to laugh and jump about and say you're happy because you're not sad. By two-faced Janus, Nature has made some strange people in her time. Some peer out through screwed-up eyes and laugh at everything, like parrots at a bagpipe player. Others look so sour that they won't show their teeth in a smile, even if wise old Nestor swore the joke was funny.
Here comes Bassanio, your most noble kinsman, / Gratiano, and Lorenzo. Fare ye well. / We leave you now with better company.
Here comes Bassanio, your most noble relative, with Gratiano and Lorenzo. Goodbye. We'll leave you now with better company.
I would have stay'd till I had made you merry, / If worthier friends had not prevented me.
I'd have stayed until I'd cheered you up, if worthier friends hadn't got here first.
Your worth is very dear in my regard. / I take it your own business calls on you, / And you embrace th' occasion to depart.
I value you very highly. I think your own business is calling you, and you're seizing the chance to leave.
Good signiors both, when shall we laugh? Say, when? / You grow exceeding strange. Must it be so?
Good gentlemen, when shall we have some fun together? Tell me, when? You've become real strangers. Must it be like this?
We'll make our leisures to attend on yours.
We'll make our free time fit with yours.
My Lord Bassanio, since you have found Antonio, / We two will leave you, but at dinner-time / I pray you have in mind where we must meet.
My Lord Bassanio, now that you've found Antonio, we two will leave you. But please remember where we're meeting at dinner-time.
You look not well, Signior Antonio, / You have too much respect upon the world. / They lose it that do buy it with much care. / Believe me, you are marvellously chang'd.
You don't look well, Signior Antonio. You take the world's business too seriously. People who buy it with so much worry lose it. Believe me, you've changed amazingly.
I hold the world but as the world, Gratiano, / A stage, where every man must play a part, / And mine a sad one.
I see the world as just what it is, Gratiano: a stage where everyone has to play a part, and mine is a sad one.

Let me play the fool, / With mirth and laughter let old wrinkles come, / And let my liver rather heat with wine / Than my heart cool with mortifying groans. / Why should a man whose blood is warm within / Sit like his grandsire cut in alabaster? / Sleep when he wakes? And creep into the jaundice / By being peevish? I tell thee what, Antonio, / (I love thee, and 'tis my love that speaks): / There are a sort of men whose visages / Do cream and mantle like a standing pond, / And do a wilful stillness entertain, / With purpose to be dress'd in an opinion / Of wisdom, gravity, profound conceit, / As who should say, "I am Sir Oracle, / And when I ope my lips, let no dog bark." / O my Antonio, I do know of these / That therefore only are reputed wise / For saying nothing; when, I am very sure, / If they should speak, would almost damn those ears / Which, hearing them, would call their brothers fools. / I'll tell thee more of this another time. / But fish not with this melancholy bait / For this fool gudgeon, this opinion. / Come, good Lorenzo. Fare ye well a while. / I'll end my exhortation after dinner.

Let me play the fool, then. Let me get old wrinkles from fun and laughter, and let my liver be heated with wine rather than my heart chilled by deadly groaning. Why should a man with warm blood in him sit like a marble statue of his grandfather? Sleep when he's awake, and make himself ill with jaundice by being grumpy? I'll tell you what, Antonio, and I say it because I love you. There's a kind of man whose face is covered with a scum, like a stagnant pond. They keep deliberately still so that people will think they are wise, serious and deep. It's as if they were saying, "I am Sir Oracle, and when I open my mouth, let no dog bark." Oh, my Antonio, I know men like that who are thought wise only because they say nothing. I'm quite sure that if they did speak, their listeners would call them fools and be damned for it. I'll tell you more about this another time. But don't use your gloominess as bait to catch this worthless fish, a reputation for wisdom. Come, good Lorenzo. Goodbye for now. I'll finish my sermon after dinner.
Well, we will leave you then till dinner-time. / I must be one of these same dumb wise men, / For Gratiano never lets me speak.
Well, we'll leave you until dinner-time, then. I'll have to be one of these silent wise men, because Gratiano never lets me speak.
Well, keep me company but two years moe, / Thou shalt not know the sound of thine own tongue.
Well, keep me company for two more years and you'll forget the sound of your own voice.
Fare you well. I'll grow a talker for this gear.
Goodbye. I'll become a talker after this lesson.
Thanks, i' faith, for silence is only commendable / In a neat's tongue dried, and a maid not vendible.
Thanks, honestly, because silence is only worth having in a dried ox tongue and in a girl nobody wants to marry.

Gratiano speaks an infinite deal of nothing, more than any man in all / Venice. His reasons are as two grains of wheat hid in two bushels of / chaff: you shall seek all day ere you find them, and when you have them / they are not worth the search.

Gratiano talks an endless amount of nothing, more than any man in Venice. His sensible points are like two grains of wheat hidden in two bushels of chaff: you'll search all day before you find them, and when you have them they aren't worth the search.
Well, tell me now what lady is the same / To whom you swore a secret pilgrimage, / That you today promis'd to tell me of?
Well, tell me now about this lady you swore to make a secret pilgrimage to, the one you promised to tell me about today.

'Tis not unknown to you, Antonio, / How much I have disabled mine estate / By something showing a more swelling port / Than my faint means would grant continuance. / Nor do I now make moan to be abridg'd / From such a noble rate, but my chief care / Is to come fairly off from the great debts / Wherein my time, something too prodigal, / Hath left me gag'd. To you, Antonio, / I owe the most in money and in love, / And from your love I have a warranty / To unburden all my plots and purposes / How to get clear of all the debts I owe.

You know well enough, Antonio, how much I've damaged my finances by living in a grander style than my small income could keep up. I'm not complaining now about having to cut back from such a noble way of life. My main concern is to get honourably clear of the large debts my rather wasteful youth has left me tied to. To you, Antonio, I owe the most, in money and in love, and your love gives me the right to share all my plans and schemes for getting free of all my debts.

I pray you, good Bassanio, let me know it; / And if it stand, as you yourself still do, / Within the eye of honour, be assur'd / My purse, my person, my extremest means / Lie all unlock'd to your occasions.
Please, good Bassanio, tell me. And if your plan is honourable, as you always are, you can be sure that my money, my person and everything I have are all open to your needs.

In my school-days, when I had lost one shaft, / I shot his fellow of the self-same flight / The self-same way, with more advised watch / To find the other forth; and by adventuring both / I oft found both. I urge this childhood proof / Because what follows is pure innocence. / I owe you much, and, like a wilful youth, / That which I owe is lost. But if you please / To shoot another arrow that self way / Which you did shoot the first, I do not doubt, / As I will watch the aim, or to find both, / Or bring your latter hazard back again, / And thankfully rest debtor for the first.

When I was a schoolboy and lost an arrow, I used to shoot another of the same kind in the same direction, watching more carefully, to find the first. By risking both, I often found both. I mention this childhood example because what follows is just as innocent. I owe you a lot, and, like a reckless young man, I've lost what I owe. But if you're willing to shoot another arrow in the same direction as the first, I'm sure that, as I'll be watching the target, I'll either find both or bring back your second stake and stay gratefully in your debt for the first.

You know me well, and herein spend but time / To wind about my love with circumstance; / And out of doubt you do me now more wrong / In making question of my uttermost / Than if you had made waste of all I have. / Then do but say to me what I should do / That in your knowledge may by me be done, / And I am prest unto it. Therefore, speak.

You know me well, and you're only wasting time by going round the houses about my love. In fact, you do me more wrong by doubting that I'll do my utmost than if you'd wasted everything I have. So just tell me what you know I can do, and I'm ready to do it. So, speak.

In Belmont is a lady richly left, / And she is fair, and, fairer than that word, / Of wondrous virtues. Sometimes from her eyes / I did receive fair speechless messages: / Her name is Portia, nothing undervalu'd / To Cato's daughter, Brutus' Portia. / Nor is the wide world ignorant of her worth, / For the four winds blow in from every coast / Renowned suitors, and her sunny locks / Hang on her temples like a golden fleece, / Which makes her seat of Belmont Colchos' strond, / And many Jasons come in quest of her. / O my Antonio, had I but the means / To hold a rival place with one of them, / I have a mind presages me such thrift / That I should questionless be fortunate.

In Belmont there's a lady who has inherited a fortune. She's beautiful and, better than beautiful, wonderfully good. Sometimes her eyes have sent me lovely silent messages. Her name is Portia, and she is worth no less than Cato's daughter Portia, the wife of Brutus. The whole world knows her worth, because the four winds blow in famous suitors from every shore. Her shining hair hangs on her forehead like the golden fleece, which makes her home at Belmont like the shore of Colchis, and many Jasons come to win her. Oh, my Antonio, if I only had the money to compete with one of them, I have a feeling that tells me I'd be so successful that I'd certainly win her.

Thou know'st that all my fortunes are at sea; / Neither have I money nor commodity / To raise a present sum, therefore go forth / Try what my credit can in Venice do; / That shall be rack'd even to the uttermost, / To furnish thee to Belmont to fair Portia. / Go presently inquire, and so will I, / Where money is, and I no question make / To have it of my trust or for my sake.

You know all my wealth is at sea. I have neither money nor goods to raise a sum right now. So go out and see what my credit can do in Venice. It will be stretched to the limit to equip you to go to Belmont and beautiful Portia. Go and find out at once where there's money to be had, and so will I. I'm sure I'll get it, either on my credit or as a personal favour.
By my troth, Nerissa, my little body is aweary of this great world.
Honestly, Nerissa, my little body is tired of this great world.

You would be, sweet madam, if your miseries were in the same abundance / as your good fortunes are. And yet, for aught I see, they are as sick / that surfeit with too much as they that starve with nothing. It is no / mean happiness, therefore, to be seated in the mean. Superfluity come / sooner by white hairs, but competency lives longer.

You would be, sweet madam, if your troubles were as plentiful as your good fortune. And yet, as far as I can see, people who stuff themselves with too much are as sick as people who starve with nothing. So it's no small happiness to be placed in the middle. Excess gives you white hair sooner, but having just enough helps you live longer.
They would be better if well followed.
They'd be better if they were followed.

If to do were as easy as to know what were good to do, chapels had been / churches, and poor men's cottages princes' palaces. It is a good divine / that follows his own instructions; I can easier teach twenty what were / good to be done than to be one of the twenty to follow mine own / teaching. The brain may devise laws for the blood, but a hot temper / leaps o'er a cold decree; such a hare is madness the youth, to skip / o'er the meshes of good counsel the cripple. But this reasoning is not / in the fashion to choose me a husband. O me, the word "choose"! I may / neither choose who I would nor refuse who I dislike, so is the will of / a living daughter curb'd by the will of a dead father. Is it not hard, / Nerissa, that I cannot choose one, nor refuse none?

If doing good were as easy as knowing what's good to do, little chapels would be great churches and poor men's cottages would be princes' palaces. It's a good priest who follows his own sermons. I find it easier to teach twenty people what they ought to do than to be one of the twenty and follow my own teaching. The mind can make laws to control the passions, but a hot temper leaps over a cold rule. Young people are like a mad hare, skipping over the nets of good advice laid by old cripples. But this reasoning won't help me choose a husband. Oh dear, that word "choose"! I can't choose whom I want or refuse whom I dislike: that's how the will of a living daughter is held back by the will of a dead father. Isn't it hard, Nerissa, that I can't choose one or refuse any?

Your father was ever virtuous, and holy men at their death have good / inspirations. Therefore the lott'ry that he hath devised in these three / chests of gold, silver, and lead, whereof who chooses his meaning / chooses you, will no doubt never be chosen by any rightly but one who / you shall rightly love. But what warmth is there in your affection / towards any of these princely suitors that are already come?

Your father was always a good man, and holy men have good inspirations when they are dying. So this lottery he has set up with three caskets of gold, silver and lead, where whoever picks the one he meant wins you, will surely never be chosen correctly by anyone except someone you will truly love. But how warm are your feelings towards any of these princely suitors who have already come?
I pray thee over-name them, and as thou namest them, I will describe / them, and according to my description level at my affection.
Please go through their names, and as you name them, I'll describe them. Then from my description you can guess how I feel.
First, there is the Neapolitan prince.
First, there's the prince from Naples.

Ay, that's a colt indeed, for he doth nothing but talk of his horse, / and he makes it a great appropriation to his own good parts that he can / shoe him himself. I am much afeard my lady his mother play'd false with / a smith.

Yes, he's a real colt, because he does nothing but talk about his horse. He thinks it's a great credit to his own talents that he can shoe it himself. I'm very afraid his lady mother had an affair with a blacksmith.
Then is there the County Palatine.

He doth nothing but frown, as who should say "And you will not have me, / choose." He hears merry tales and smiles not. I fear he will prove the / weeping philosopher when he grows old, being so full of unmannerly / sadness in his youth. I had rather be married to a death's-head with a / bone in his mouth than to either of these. God defend me from these / two!

He does nothing but frown, as if to say, "If you don't want me, choose someone else." He hears funny stories and doesn't smile. I'm afraid he'll become the weeping philosopher when he's old, since he's so rudely gloomy while he's young. I'd rather be married to a skull with a bone in its mouth than to either of these. God protect me from these two!
How say you by the French lord, Monsieur Le Bon?
What do you say about the French lord, Monsieur Le Bon?

God made him, and therefore let him pass for a man. In truth, I know it / is a sin to be a mocker, but he! why, he hath a horse better than the / Neapolitan's, a better bad habit of frowning than the Count Palatine. / He is every man in no man. If a throstle sing, he falls straight / a-cap'ring. He will fence with his own shadow. If I should marry him, I / should marry twenty husbands. If he would despise me, I would forgive / him, for if he love me to madness, I shall never requite him.

God made him, so let him count as a man. Honestly, I know it's a sin to mock people, but him! Why, he has a better horse than the Neapolitan and a better bad habit of frowning than the Count Palatine. He's every man and no man. If a thrush sings, he starts dancing at once. He'd fence with his own shadow. If I married him, I'd be marrying twenty husbands. If he despised me, I'd forgive him, because if he loved me madly, I'd never love him back.
What say you then to Falconbridge, the young baron of England?
What do you say, then, to Falconbridge, the young English baron?

You know I say nothing to him, for he understands not me, nor I him: he / hath neither Latin, French, nor Italian, and you will come into the / court and swear that I have a poor pennyworth in the English. He is a / proper man's picture; but alas, who can converse with a dumb-show? How / oddly he is suited! I think he bought his doublet in Italy, his round / hose in France, his bonnet in Germany, and his behaviour everywhere.

You know I say nothing to him, because he doesn't understand me and I don't understand him. He has no Latin, French or Italian, and you could swear in court that I have very little English. He's a handsome figure of a man, but who can talk to a mime show? And how strangely he dresses! I think he bought his jacket in Italy, his breeches in France, his hat in Germany and his manners everywhere.
What think you of the Scottish lord, his neighbour?
What do you think of the Scottish lord, his neighbour?

That he hath a neighbourly charity in him, for he borrowed a box of the / ear of the Englishman, and swore he would pay him again when he was / able. I think the Frenchman became his surety, and seal'd under for / another.

That he's a charitable neighbour, because he borrowed a box on the ear from the Englishman and swore he'd pay him back when he could. I think the Frenchman guaranteed the debt and signed up for another blow.
How like you the young German, the Duke of Saxony's nephew?
How do you like the young German, the Duke of Saxony's nephew?

Very vilely in the morning when he is sober, and most vilely in the / afternoon when he is drunk: when he is best, he is a little worse than / a man, and when he is worst, he is little better than a beast. And the / worst fall that ever fell, I hope I shall make shift to go without him.

Very badly in the morning when he's sober, and even worse in the afternoon when he's drunk. At his best he's a little worse than a man, and at his worst he's a little better than an animal. Even if the worst happens, I hope I'll manage to do without him.
If he should offer to choose, and choose the right casket, you should / refuse to perform your father's will, if you should refuse to accept / him.
If he offered to choose, and chose the right casket, you'd be refusing to carry out your father's will if you refused to accept him.

Therefore, for fear of the worst, I pray thee set a deep glass of / Rhenish wine on the contrary casket, for if the devil be within and / that temptation without, I know he will choose it. I will do anything, / Nerissa, ere I will be married to a sponge.

So, to be safe, please put a large glass of Rhine wine on the wrong casket. If the devil were inside it and that temptation outside, I know he'd choose it. I'll do anything, Nerissa, rather than marry a sponge.

You need not fear, lady, the having any of these lords. They have / acquainted me with their determinations, which is indeed to return to / their home, and to trouble you with no more suit, unless you may be won / by some other sort than your father's imposition, depending on the / caskets.

You needn't be afraid of getting any of these lords, madam. They've told me what they've decided, which is to go home and not trouble you with any more wooing, unless you can be won in some other way than the caskets your father imposed.

If I live to be as old as Sibylla, I will die as chaste as Diana, / unless I be obtained by the manner of my father's will. I am glad this / parcel of wooers are so reasonable, for there is not one among them but / I dote on his very absence. And I pray God grant them a fair departure.

Even if I live as long as the Sibyl, I'll die as chaste as the goddess Diana unless I'm won the way my father's will lays down. I'm glad this bunch of wooers is so sensible, because there's not one of them whose absence I don't adore. I pray God gives them a good journey home.
Do you not remember, lady, in your father's time, a Venetian, a scholar / and a soldier, that came hither in company of the Marquis of / Montferrat?
Don't you remember, madam, a Venetian who came here in your father's time, a scholar and a soldier, with the Marquis of Montferrat?
Yes, yes, it was Bassanio, as I think, so was he call'd.
Yes, yes, it was Bassanio, I think. That was his name.
True, madam. He, of all the men that ever my foolish eyes look'd upon, / was the best deserving a fair lady.
That's right, madam. Of all the men my foolish eyes have ever looked at, he was the one who most deserved a beautiful lady.
I remember him well, and I remember him worthy of thy praise.
I remember him well, and I remember he was worthy of your praise.
The four strangers seek for you, madam, to take their leave. And there / is a forerunner come from a fifth, the Prince of Morocco, who brings / word the Prince his master will be here tonight.
The four foreign gentlemen are looking for you, madam, to say goodbye. And a messenger has arrived from a fifth, the Prince of Morocco, who says the Prince his master will be here tonight.

If I could bid the fifth welcome with so good heart as I can bid the / other four farewell, I should be glad of his approach. If he have the / condition of a saint and the complexion of a devil, I had rather he / should shrive me than wive me. Come, Nerissa. Sirrah, go before. Whiles / we shut the gate upon one wooer, another knocks at the door.

If I could welcome the fifth as gladly as I can say goodbye to the other four, I'd be glad he was coming. If he has the character of a saint and the complexion of a devil, I'd rather he heard my confession than married me. Come, Nerissa. You, go ahead. While we shut the gate on one wooer, another knocks at the door.
For the which, as I told you, Antonio shall be bound.
And for that, as I told you, Antonio will sign the bond.
Antonio will sign the bond. Well.
May you stead me? Will you pleasure me? Shall I know your answer?
Can you help me? Will you do me this favour? May I have your answer?
Three thousand ducats for three months, and Antonio bound.
Three thousand ducats for three months, and Antonio signs the bond.
Have you heard any imputation to the contrary?
Have you heard anyone suggest otherwise?

Ho, no, no, no, no: my meaning in saying he is a good man is to have / you understand me that he is sufficient. Yet his means are in / supposition: he hath an argosy bound to Tripolis, another to the / Indies. I understand, moreover, upon the Rialto, he hath a third at / Mexico, a fourth for England, and other ventures he hath squandered / abroad. But ships are but boards, sailors but men; there be land-rats / and water-rats, water-thieves and land-thieves—I mean pirates—and then / there is the peril of waters, winds, and rocks. The man is, / notwithstanding, sufficient. Three thousand ducats. I think I may take / his bond.

Oh, no, no, no, no. When I say he's a good man, I mean that he's good for the money. But his wealth is uncertain. He has a merchant ship bound for Tripoli and another for the West Indies. I've also heard on the Rialto that he has a third in Mexico, a fourth on its way to England, and other ventures scattered abroad. But ships are only planks and sailors only men. There are land-rats and water-rats, water-thieves and land-thieves, I mean pirates, and then there's the danger of the sea, the winds and the rocks. All the same, the man is good for it. Three thousand ducats. I think I can accept his bond.
You can be sure you can.
I will be assured I may. And that I may be assured, I will bethink me. / May I speak with Antonio?
I'll make sure I can. And to make sure, I'll think it over. May I speak with Antonio?
If it please you to dine with us.
If you'd like to dine with us.

Yes, to smell pork, to eat of the habitation which your prophet, the / Nazarite, conjured the devil into. I will buy with you, sell with you, / talk with you, walk with you, and so following; but I will not eat with / you, drink with you, nor pray with you. What news on the Rialto? Who is / he comes here?

Yes, to smell pork, and eat the animal your prophet from Nazareth sent the devil into. I'll buy with you, sell with you, talk with you, walk with you and so on, but I won't eat with you, drink with you or pray with you. What's the news on the Rialto? Who's this coming?

[Aside] How like a fawning publican he looks! / I hate him for he is a Christian, / But more for that in low simplicity / He lends out money gratis, and brings down / The rate of usance here with us in Venice. / If I can catch him once upon the hip, / I will feed fat the ancient grudge I bear him. / He hates our sacred nation, and he rails, / Even there where merchants most do congregate, / On me, my bargains, and my well-won thrift, / Which he calls interest. Cursed be my tribe / If I forgive him!

[Aside] He looks just like a grovelling tax collector! I hate him because he's a Christian, but even more because in his humble foolishness he lends money without charging interest and brings down the rate of interest here in Venice. If I can ever get him at a disadvantage, I'll fully feed the old grudge I hold against him. He hates our sacred people, and he abuses me, my dealings and my hard-earned profits, which he calls interest, right where the merchants gather most. Cursed be my people if I forgive him!

I am debating of my present store, / And by the near guess of my memory / I cannot instantly raise up the gross / Of full three thousand ducats. What of that? / Tubal, a wealthy Hebrew of my tribe, / Will furnish me. But soft! how many months / Do you desire? [To Antonio] Rest you fair, good signior, / Your worship was the last man in our mouths.

I'm working out how much cash I have to hand, and as near as I can remember, I can't raise the whole three thousand ducats at once. What does that matter? Tubal, a wealthy Hebrew of my people, will supply me. But wait, how many months do you want? [To Antonio] Good day to you, good sir. We were just talking about you.

Shylock, albeit I neither lend nor borrow / By taking nor by giving of excess, / Yet to supply the ripe wants of my friend, / I'll break a custom. [To Bassanio] Is he yet possess'd / How much ye would?
Shylock, although I neither lend nor borrow by taking or paying interest, I'll break my habit to meet my friend's urgent needs. [To Bassanio] Does he know yet how much you want?
I had forgot, three months, you told me so. / Well then, your bond. And let me see, but hear you, / Methought you said you neither lend nor borrow / Upon advantage.
I'd forgotten. Three months, you told me so. Well then, your bond. Let me see. But listen, I thought you said you neither lend nor borrow at interest.
When Jacob graz'd his uncle Laban's sheep,— / This Jacob from our holy Abram was / As his wise mother wrought in his behalf, / The third possessor; ay, he was the third.
When Jacob grazed his uncle Laban's sheep, this Jacob was the third heir after our holy Abraham, thanks to his wise mother's scheming. Yes, he was the third.
And what of him? Did he take interest?
And what about him? Did he charge interest?

No, not take interest, not, as you would say, / Directly interest; mark what Jacob did. / When Laban and himself were compromis'd / That all the eanlings which were streak'd and pied / Should fall as Jacob's hire, the ewes being rank / In end of autumn turned to the rams, / And when the work of generation was / Between these woolly breeders in the act, / The skilful shepherd pill'd me certain wands, / And in the doing of the deed of kind, / He stuck them up before the fulsome ewes, / Who then conceiving did in eaning time / Fall parti-colour'd lambs, and those were Jacob's. / This was a way to thrive, and he was blest; / And thrift is blessing if men steal it not.

No, he didn't charge interest, not what you'd call interest directly. Listen to what Jacob did. Laban and he had agreed that all the newborn lambs that were streaked and spotted would be Jacob's wages. At the end of autumn the ewes were on heat and went to the rams, and when these woolly breeders were mating, the clever shepherd peeled some sticks for himself, and while they were doing the deed of nature he stuck them up in front of the lusty ewes. They conceived then, and at lambing time gave birth to multicoloured lambs, and those were Jacob's. This was a way to prosper, and he was blessed. Profit is a blessing, as long as men don't steal it.

This was a venture, sir, that Jacob serv'd for, / A thing not in his power to bring to pass, / But sway'd and fashion'd by the hand of heaven. / Was this inserted to make interest good? / Or is your gold and silver ewes and rams?

That was a risk Jacob worked for, sir, something he couldn't make happen himself. It was controlled and shaped by the hand of heaven. Was this put in the Bible to make interest acceptable? Or are your gold and silver ewes and rams?
I cannot tell; I make it breed as fast. / But note me, signior.
I can't say. I make it breed as fast. But listen to me, signior.

Mark you this, Bassanio, / The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose. / An evil soul producing holy witness / Is like a villain with a smiling cheek, / A goodly apple rotten at the heart. / O, what a goodly outside falsehood hath!

Notice this, Bassanio: the devil can quote Scripture to suit himself. An evil soul calling holy writing as a witness is like a villain with a smiling face, a fine-looking apple that is rotten at the core. Oh, what a handsome outside falsehood has!
Three thousand ducats, 'tis a good round sum. / Three months from twelve, then let me see the rate.
Three thousand ducats. That's a good round sum. Three months out of twelve. Now let me work out the interest.
Well, Shylock, shall we be beholding to you?
Well, Shylock, are we going to be in your debt?

Signior Antonio, many a time and oft / In the Rialto you have rated me / About my moneys and my usances. / Still have I borne it with a patient shrug, / (For suff'rance is the badge of all our tribe.) / You call me misbeliever, cut-throat dog, / And spet upon my Jewish gaberdine, / And all for use of that which is mine own. / Well then, it now appears you need my help. / Go to, then, you come to me, and you say / "Shylock, we would have moneys." You say so: / You that did void your rheum upon my beard, / And foot me as you spurn a stranger cur / Over your threshold, moneys is your suit. / What should I say to you? Should I not say / "Hath a dog money? Is it possible / A cur can lend three thousand ducats?" Or / Shall I bend low and, in a bondman's key, / With bated breath and whisp'ring humbleness, / Say this: / "Fair sir, you spet on me on Wednesday last; / You spurn'd me such a day; another time / You call'd me dog; and for these courtesies / I'll lend you thus much moneys"?

Signior Antonio, many, many times on the Rialto you have scolded me about my money and my lending. I've always put up with it with a patient shrug, because suffering is the mark of all our people. You call me unbeliever, cut-throat dog, and spit on my Jewish cloak, and all because I use what belongs to me. Well then, now it seems you need my help. So there you are: you come to me, and you say, "Shylock, we'd like some money." You say that, you who emptied your spit on my beard and kicked me as you'd kick a stray dog out of your doorway. Money is what you're asking for. What should I say to you? Shouldn't I say, "Does a dog have money? Is it possible for a mongrel to lend three thousand ducats?" Or should I bow low and, in a slave's voice, holding my breath and whispering humbly, say this: "Fair sir, you spat on me last Wednesday. You kicked me on such and such a day. Another time you called me dog. And for these kindnesses I'll lend you this much money"?

I am as like to call thee so again, / To spet on thee again, to spurn thee too. / If thou wilt lend this money, lend it not / As to thy friends, for when did friendship take / A breed for barren metal of his friend? / But lend it rather to thine enemy, / Who if he break, thou mayst with better face / Exact the penalty.

I'm just as likely to call you that again, to spit on you again and to kick you too. If you're going to lend this money, don't lend it as if to your friends, because when did a friend ever charge his friend for lending money, which can't breed? Lend it instead to your enemy. If he fails to pay, you can more easily demand the penalty.

Why, look you how you storm! / I would be friends with you, and have your love, / Forget the shames that you have stain'd me with, / Supply your present wants, and take no doit / Of usance for my moneys, and you'll not hear me, / This is kind I offer.

Why, look how you rage! I want to be friends with you and have your love, to forget the shameful things you've done to me, to supply what you need now and charge not a penny of interest for my money, and you won't listen. This is a kind offer I'm making.

This kindness will I show. / Go with me to a notary, seal me there / Your single bond; and in a merry sport, / If you repay me not on such a day, / In such a place, such sum or sums as are / Express'd in the condition, let the forfeit / Be nominated for an equal pound / Of your fair flesh, to be cut off and taken / In what part of your body pleaseth me.

I'll show you this kindness. Come with me to a lawyer and sign a bond there with no other guarantor. And as a joke, if you don't repay me on such a day, in such a place, the sum or sums stated in the contract, let the penalty be a pound of your fair flesh, to be cut off and taken from whatever part of your body I please.
Content, in faith, I'll seal to such a bond, / And say there is much kindness in the Jew.
Agreed, honestly. I'll sign a bond like that and say the Jew is very kind.
You shall not seal to such a bond for me, / I'll rather dwell in my necessity.
You won't sign a bond like that for me. I'd rather go on being poor.
Why, fear not, man, I will not forfeit it, / Within these two months, that's a month before / This bond expires, I do expect return / Of thrice three times the value of this bond.
Why, don't be afraid, man. I won't fail to pay. Within the next two months, a month before this bond falls due, I expect to receive nine times its value.

O father Abram, what these Christians are, / Whose own hard dealings teaches them suspect / The thoughts of others. Pray you, tell me this, / If he should break his day, what should I gain / By the exaction of the forfeiture? / A pound of man's flesh, taken from a man, / Is not so estimable, profitable neither, / As flesh of muttons, beefs, or goats. I say, / To buy his favour, I extend this friendship. / If he will take it, so. If not, adieu, / And for my love I pray you wrong me not.

Oh, father Abraham, what these Christians are like! Their own hard dealing teaches them to suspect what others mean. Please tell me this: if he missed the day for payment, what would I gain by taking the penalty? A pound of human flesh, taken from a man, is not as valuable or as useful as the flesh of sheep, cows or goats. I tell you, I'm offering this friendship to win his goodwill. If he'll take it, good. If not, goodbye. And in return for my friendship, please don't think badly of me.
Yes, Shylock, I will seal unto this bond.
Yes, Shylock, I'll sign this bond.

Then meet me forthwith at the notary's, / Give him direction for this merry bond, / And I will go and purse the ducats straight, / See to my house left in the fearful guard / Of an unthrifty knave, and presently / I'll be with you.

Then meet me straight away at the lawyer's. Give him instructions for this merry bond, and I'll go and fetch the ducats at once, check on my house, which I've left in the unreliable care of a careless servant, and I'll be with you shortly.
This Hebrew will turn Christian; he grows kind.
This Hebrew will turn Christian. He's getting kind.
I like not fair terms and a villain's mind.
I don't like fair words from someone with a villain's mind.
Come on; in this there can be no dismay; / My ships come home a month before the day.
Come on, there's nothing to fear in this. My ships will come home a month before the day.

Mislike me not for my complexion, / The shadowed livery of the burnish'd sun, / To whom I am a neighbour, and near bred. / Bring me the fairest creature northward born, / Where Phœbus' fire scarce thaws the icicles, / And let us make incision for your love / To prove whose blood is reddest, his or mine. / I tell thee, lady, this aspect of mine / Hath fear'd the valiant; by my love I swear / The best-regarded virgins of our clime / Have lov'd it too. I would not change this hue, / Except to steal your thoughts, my gentle queen.

Don't dislike me for the colour of my skin, the dark uniform of the blazing sun, whose neighbour I am and close to whom I was raised. Bring me the fairest man born in the north, where the sun's fire hardly melts the icicles, and let's cut ourselves for your love to prove whose blood is reddest, his or mine. I tell you, lady, this face of mine has frightened brave men, and I swear by my love that the most admired young women of my country have loved it too. I wouldn't change this colour, except to win your thoughts, my gentle queen.

In terms of choice I am not solely led / By nice direction of a maiden's eyes; / Besides, the lott'ry of my destiny / Bars me the right of voluntary choosing. / But if my father had not scanted me / And hedg'd me by his wit to yield myself / His wife who wins me by that means I told you, / Yourself, renowned Prince, then stood as fair / As any comer I have look'd on yet / For my affection.

In choosing, I'm not guided only by what a girl's fussy eyes tell her. And anyway, the lottery that decides my fate denies me the right to choose for myself. But if my father hadn't limited me, and fenced me in with his scheme so that I must give myself as wife to whoever wins me in the way I told you, you yourself, famous Prince, would have as good a chance of my love as any suitor I've seen so far.

Even for that I thank you. / Therefore I pray you lead me to the caskets / To try my fortune. By this scimitar / That slew the Sophy and a Persian prince, / That won three fields of Sultan Solyman, / I would o'erstare the sternest eyes that look, / Outbrave the heart most daring on the earth, / Pluck the young sucking cubs from the she-bear, / Yea, mock the lion when he roars for prey, / To win thee, lady. But, alas the while! / If Hercules and Lichas play at dice / Which is the better man, the greater throw / May turn by fortune from the weaker hand: / So is Alcides beaten by his rage, / And so may I, blind Fortune leading me, / Miss that which one unworthier may attain, / And die with grieving.

I thank you even for that. So please take me to the caskets to try my luck. By this curved sword, which killed the Shah of Persia and a Persian prince, and won three battles against Sultan Suleiman, I'd outstare the fiercest eyes in the world, outdare the boldest heart on earth, snatch suckling cubs from the mother bear, even mock the lion when he roars for his prey, to win you, lady. But, what a pity! If Hercules and his servant Lichas play dice to decide which is the better man, the higher throw may come by luck from the weaker hand. That way Hercules is beaten by his servant, and that way I, led by blind Fortune, may miss what someone less worthy may win, and die of grief.
You must take your chance, / And either not attempt to choose at all, / Or swear before you choose, if you choose wrong / Never to speak to lady afterward / In way of marriage. Therefore be advis'd.
You must take your chance. Either don't try to choose at all, or swear before you choose that if you choose wrong you'll never ask any lady to marry you afterwards. So think carefully.
Nor will not. Come, bring me unto my chance.
I won't ask anyone else. Come, take me to my chance.
First, forward to the temple. After dinner / Your hazard shall be made.
First, to the temple. After dinner you'll make your gamble.
Good fortune then, / To make me blest or cursed'st among men!
Good luck, then, to make me the most blessed or the most cursed of men!

Certainly my conscience will serve me to run from this Jew my master. / The fiend is at mine elbow and tempts me, saying to me "Gobbo, / Launcelet Gobbo, good Launcelet" or "good Gobbo," or "good Launcelet / Gobbo, use your legs, take the start, run away." My conscience says / "No; take heed, honest Launcelet, take heed, honest Gobbo" or, as / aforesaid, "honest Launcelet Gobbo, do not run, scorn running with thy / heels." Well, the most courageous fiend bids me pack. "Fia!" says the / fiend, "away!" says the fiend. "For the heavens, rouse up a brave / mind," says the fiend, "and run." Well, my conscience, hanging about / the neck of my heart, says very wisely to me "My honest friend / Launcelet, being an honest man's son"—or rather an honest woman's son, / for indeed my father did something smack, something grow to, he had a / kind of taste;—well, my conscience says "Launcelet, budge not." / "Budge," says the fiend. "Budge not," says my conscience. "Conscience," / say I, "you counsel well." "Fiend," say I, "you counsel well." To be / ruled by my conscience, I should stay with the Jew my master, who, (God / bless the mark) is a kind of devil; and, to run away from the Jew, I / should be ruled by the fiend, who (saving your reverence) is the devil / himself. Certainly the Jew is the very devil incarnation, and, in my / conscience, my conscience is but a kind of hard conscience, to offer to / counsel me to stay with the Jew. The fiend gives the more friendly / counsel. I will run, fiend, my heels are at your commandment, I will / run.

Surely my conscience will let me run away from this Jew, my master. The devil is at my elbow tempting me, saying, "Gobbo, Launcelet Gobbo, good Launcelet," or "good Gobbo," or "good Launcelet Gobbo, use your legs, get going, run away." My conscience says, "No, be careful, honest Launcelet, be careful, honest Gobbo," or, as I said before, "honest Launcelet Gobbo, don't run, kick the idea of running away." Well, the very brave devil tells me to pack my bags. "Off!" says the devil. "Away!" says the devil. "For heaven's sake, be brave," says the devil, "and run." Well, my conscience, hanging round the neck of my heart, says very wisely to me, "My honest friend Launcelet, being an honest man's son," or rather an honest woman's son, because my father did have a bit of a whiff about him, he had a certain taste for things. Well, my conscience says, "Launcelet, don't budge." "Budge," says the devil. "Don't budge," says my conscience. "Conscience," I say, "you give good advice." "Devil," I say, "you give good advice." If I do what my conscience says, I should stay with the Jew my master, who, God forgive me, is a kind of devil. And to run away from the Jew, I should do what the devil says, who, pardon me, is the devil himself. Surely the Jew is the devil in the flesh, and, on my conscience, my conscience is a pretty hard conscience to advise me to stay with the Jew. The devil gives the friendlier advice. I'll run, devil. My heels are yours to command. I'll run.
Master young man, you, I pray you; which is the way to Master Jew's?
Young master, you there, please, which is the way to Master Jew's?
[Aside] O heavens, this is my true-begotten father, who being more / than sand-blind, high-gravel blind, knows me not. I will try confusions / with him.
[Aside] Oh heavens, it's my own true father! He's more than half blind, nearly stone blind, and doesn't recognise me. I'll play some tricks on him.
Master young gentleman, I pray you, which is the way to Master Jew's?
Young master gentleman, please, which is the way to Master Jew's?
Turn up on your right hand at the next turning, but at the next turning / of all on your left; marry, at the very next turning, turn of no hand, / but turn down indirectly to the Jew's house.
Turn right at the next turning, but at the turning after that, left. Then, at the very next turning, don't turn either way, but turn down sideways to the Jew's house.
Be God's sonties, 'twill be a hard way to hit. Can you tell me whether / one Launcelet, that dwells with him, dwell with him or no?
By God's saints, that'll be a hard way to find. Can you tell me whether a man called Launcelet, who lives with him, lives with him or not?
Talk you of young Master Launcelet? [Aside] Mark me now, now will I / raise the waters. Talk you of young Master Launcelet?
Are you talking about young Master Launcelet? [Aside] Watch me now, I'll get the tears flowing. Are you talking about young Master Launcelet?
No master, sir, but a poor man's son, his father, though I say't, is an / honest exceeding poor man, and, God be thanked, well to live.
Not Master, sir, just a poor man's son. His father, though I say it myself, is an honest, very poor man and, thank God, healthy enough.
Well, let his father be what he will, we talk of young Master / Launcelet.
Well, his father can be whatever he likes, we're talking about young Master Launcelet.
Your worship's friend, and Launcelet, sir.
Your worship's friend, and just Launcelet, sir.
But I pray you, ergo, old man, ergo, I beseech you, talk you of / young Master Launcelet?
But I beg you, therefore, old man, therefore, I ask you, are you talking about young Master Launcelet?
Of Launcelet, an't please your mastership.
About Launcelet, if it please your worship.

Ergo, Master Launcelet. Talk not of Master Launcelet, father, for the / young gentleman, according to Fates and Destinies, and such odd / sayings, the Sisters Three and such branches of learning, is indeed / deceased, or, as you would say in plain terms, gone to heaven.

Therefore, Master Launcelet. Don't talk about Master Launcelet, old man, because the young gentleman, according to the Fates and Destinies and such strange sayings, the Three Sisters and such branches of learning, is in fact deceased, or, as you'd put it plainly, gone to heaven.
Marry, God forbid! The boy was the very staff of my age, my very prop.
God forbid! The boy was the very staff of my old age, my prop.
[Aside] Do I look like a cudgel or a hovel-post, a staff or a prop? / Do you know me, father?
[Aside] Do I look like a club or a fence post, a staff or a prop? Do you know me, old man?
Alack the day! I know you not, young gentleman, but I pray you tell me, / is my boy, God rest his soul, alive or dead?
Oh dear! I don't know you, young gentleman. But please tell me, is my boy, God rest his soul, alive or dead?
Do you not know me, father?
Alack, sir, I am sand-blind, I know you not.
Alas, sir, I'm half blind. I don't know you.

Nay, indeed, if you had your eyes, you might fail of the knowing me: it / is a wise father that knows his own child. Well, old man, I will tell / you news of your son. Give me your blessing, truth will come to light, / murder cannot be hid long, a man's son may, but in the end truth will / out.

No, really, even if you had your eyes you might not know me. It's a wise father who knows his own child. Well, old man, I'll give you news of your son. Give me your blessing. The truth will come to light. Murder can't be hidden long, a man's son can, but in the end the truth will come out.
Pray you, sir, stand up, I am sure you are not Launcelet my boy.
Please, sir, stand up. I'm sure you're not Launcelet my boy.
Pray you, let's have no more fooling about it, but give me your / blessing. I am Launcelet, your boy that was, your son that is, your / child that shall be.
Please, let's have no more fooling about. Just give me your blessing. I'm Launcelet, your boy that was, your son that is, your child that will be.
I cannot think you are my son.
I can't believe you're my son.
I know not what I shall think of that; but I am Launcelet, the Jew's / man, and I am sure Margery your wife is my mother.
I don't know what to think about that, but I'm Launcelet, the Jew's servant, and I'm sure your wife Margery is my mother.

Her name is Margery, indeed. I'll be sworn if thou be Launcelet, thou / art mine own flesh and blood. Lord worshipped might he be, what a beard / hast thou got! Thou hast got more hair on thy chin than Dobbin my / fill-horse has on his tail.

Her name is Margery, it's true. I'll swear that if you're Launcelet, you're my own flesh and blood. Lord be praised, what a beard you've grown! You've got more hair on your chin than my cart-horse Dobbin has on his tail.
It should seem, then, that Dobbin's tail grows backward. I am sure he / had more hair on his tail than I have on my face when I last saw him.
Then it seems Dobbin's tail grows backwards. I'm sure he had more hair on his tail than I have on my face when I last saw him.
Lord, how art thou changed! How dost thou and thy master agree? I have / brought him a present. How 'gree you now?
Lord, how you've changed! How do you and your master get on? I've brought him a present. How do you get on now?

Well, well. But for mine own part, as I have set up my rest to run / away, so I will not rest till I have run some ground. My master's a / very Jew. Give him a present! Give him a halter. I am famished in his / service. You may tell every finger I have with my ribs. Father, I am / glad you are come, give me your present to one Master Bassanio, who / indeed gives rare new liveries. If I serve not him, I will run as far / as God has any ground. O rare fortune, here comes the man! To him, / father; for I am a Jew, if I serve the Jew any longer.

Fine, fine. But as for me, since I've made up my mind to run away, I won't rest till I've run a good distance. My master's a real Jew. Give him a present? Give him a noose! I'm starving in his service. You can count every finger I have with my ribs. Father, I'm glad you've come. Give your present to a Master Bassanio, who really does give fine new uniforms. If I can't serve him, I'll run as far as God has land. What luck, here comes the man! Go to him, father, because I'll be a Jew myself if I serve the Jew any longer.

You may do so, but let it be so hasted that supper be ready at the / farthest by five of the clock. See these letters delivered, put the / liveries to making, and desire Gratiano to come anon to my lodging.

You can do that, but be quick about it, so that supper is ready by five o'clock at the latest. See that these letters are delivered, get the uniforms made, and ask Gratiano to come to my lodging soon.
Gramercy, wouldst thou aught with me?
Thank you. Do you want something from me?
Here's my son, sir, a poor boy.
Here's my son, sir, a poor boy.
Not a poor boy, sir, but the rich Jew's man, that would, sir, as my / father shall specify.
Not a poor boy, sir, but the rich Jew's servant, who would like, sir, as my father will explain.
He hath a great infection, sir, as one would say, to serve.
He has a great infection, sir, as you might say, to serve.
Indeed the short and the long is, I serve the Jew, and have a desire, / as my father shall specify.
In fact, the short and the long of it is, I serve the Jew, and I have a desire, as my father will explain.
His master and he (saving your worship's reverence) are scarce / cater-cousins.
His master and he, begging your worship's pardon, are hardly the best of friends.
To be brief, the very truth is that the Jew, having done me wrong, doth / cause me, as my father, being I hope an old man, shall frutify unto / you.
To be brief, the honest truth is that the Jew, having treated me badly, makes me, as my father, who is an old man I hope, will fructify to you.
I have here a dish of doves that I would bestow upon your worship, and / my suit is—
I have here a dish of doves I'd like to give your worship, and my request is—
In very brief, the suit is impertinent to myself, as your worship shall / know by this honest old man, and though I say it, though old man, yet / poor man, my father.
In very short, the request is impertinent to me, as your worship will learn from this honest old man, and, though I say it myself, though he's an old man, he's a poor man, and my father.
One speak for both. What would you?
One of you speak for both. What do you want?
That is the very defect of the matter, sir.
That's the whole defect of the matter, sir.

I know thee well; thou hast obtain'd thy suit. / Shylock thy master spoke with me this day, / And hath preferr'd thee, if it be preferment / To leave a rich Jew's service to become / The follower of so poor a gentleman.

I know you well. You've got your wish. Your master Shylock spoke with me today and has recommended you, if it's a promotion to leave a rich Jew's service and become the servant of such a poor gentleman.
The old proverb is very well parted between my master Shylock and you, / sir: you have "the grace of God", sir, and he hath "enough".
The old proverb is nicely shared out between my master Shylock and you, sir. You have "the grace of God", sir, and he has "enough".
Thou speak'st it well. Go, father, with thy son. / Take leave of thy old master, and inquire / My lodging out. [To a Servant] Give him a livery / More guarded than his fellows'; see it done.
Well said. Go, old man, with your son. Say goodbye to your old master, and find out where I'm staying. [To a Servant] Give him a uniform with more braid on it than the others'. See that it's done.

Father, in. I cannot get a service, no! I have ne'er a tongue in my / head! [Looking on his palm] Well, if any man in Italy have a fairer / table which doth offer to swear upon a book, I shall have good fortune; / go to, here's a simple line of life. Here's a small trifle of wives, / alas, fifteen wives is nothing; eleven widows and nine maids is a / simple coming-in for one man. And then to scape drowning thrice, and to / be in peril of my life with the edge of a feather-bed; here are simple / 'scapes. Well, if Fortune be a woman, she's a good wench for this gear. / Father, come; I'll take my leave of the Jew in the twinkling.

Father, come in. I can't get a job, no! I haven't got a tongue in my head! [Looking at his palm] Well, if any man in Italy has a better palm to swear on the Bible with, I'll have good luck. Look, here's a plain line of life. Here's a small handful of wives. Oh, fifteen wives is nothing. Eleven widows and nine virgins is a modest income for one man. And then to escape drowning three times, and to be in danger of my life on the edge of a feather bed: here are some simple escapes! Well, if Fortune's a woman, she's a good girl for this business. Come on, father. I'll take my leave of the Jew in a flash.
I pray thee, good Leonardo, think on this. / These things being bought and orderly bestow'd, / Return in haste, for I do feast tonight / My best esteem'd acquaintance; hie thee, go.
Please, good Leonardo, remember this. When these things are bought and properly stowed, come back quickly, because tonight I'm giving a feast for my most valued friends. Hurry, go.
My best endeavours shall be done herein.
I have a request to make of you.
You must not deny me, I must go with you to Belmont.
You mustn't refuse me. I must go with you to Belmont.

Why, then you must. But hear thee, Gratiano, / Thou art too wild, too rude, and bold of voice, / Parts that become thee happily enough, / And in such eyes as ours appear not faults; / But where thou art not known, why there they show / Something too liberal. Pray thee, take pain / To allay with some cold drops of modesty / Thy skipping spirit, lest through thy wild behaviour / I be misconst'red in the place I go to, / And lose my hopes.

Why, then you must. But listen, Gratiano. You're too wild, too rough and too loud. Those qualities suit you well enough, and to eyes like ours they don't seem like faults. But where you aren't known they look a little too free. Please make an effort to cool your bouncing spirits with a few cold drops of good behaviour, in case your wild behaviour makes people misjudge me where I'm going, and I lose my hopes.

Signior Bassanio, hear me. / If I do not put on a sober habit, / Talk with respect, and swear but now and then, / Wear prayer-books in my pocket, look demurely, / Nay more, while grace is saying, hood mine eyes / Thus with my hat, and sigh, and say "amen"; / Use all the observance of civility / Like one well studied in a sad ostent / To please his grandam, never trust me more.

Signior Bassanio, listen to me. If I don't put on serious clothes, talk respectfully and swear only now and then, carry prayer books in my pocket and look modest, even more, cover my eyes with my hat like this while grace is being said, and sigh, and say "amen", and observe all the rules of good manners, like someone who has practised looking solemn to please his grandmother, then never trust me again.
Well, we shall see your bearing.
Well, we'll see how you behave.
Nay, but I bar tonight, you shall not gauge me / By what we do tonight.
No, but I don't count tonight. You mustn't judge me by what we do tonight.
No, that were pity. / I would entreat you rather to put on / Your boldest suit of mirth, for we have friends / That purpose merriment. But fare you well, / I have some business.
No, that would be a pity. I'd rather ask you to put on your boldest suit of fun, because we have friends who intend to have a good time. But goodbye. I have some business.
And I must to Lorenzo and the rest, / But we will visit you at supper-time.
And I must go to Lorenzo and the others, but we'll come to see you at supper-time.

I am sorry thou wilt leave my father so. / Our house is hell, and thou, a merry devil, / Didst rob it of some taste of tediousness. / But fare thee well, there is a ducat for thee, / And, Launcelet, soon at supper shalt thou see / Lorenzo, who is thy new master's guest. / Give him this letter, do it secretly. / And so farewell. I would not have my father / See me in talk with thee.

I'm sorry you're leaving my father like this. Our house is hell, and you, a merry devil, took away some of its boredom. But goodbye. Here's a ducat for you. And, Launcelet, at supper soon you'll see Lorenzo, who is your new master's guest. Give him this letter, and do it secretly. And so goodbye. I don't want my father to see me talking to you.

Adieu! tears exhibit my tongue, most beautiful pagan, most sweet Jew! / If a Christian do not play the knave and get thee, I am much deceived. / But, adieu! These foolish drops do something drown my manly spirit. / Adieu!

Goodbye! Tears are my tongue, most beautiful heathen, most sweet Jew! If a Christian doesn't play the rogue and get you, I'm very much mistaken. But goodbye! These foolish drops are rather drowning my manly spirit. Goodbye!

Alack, what heinous sin is it in me / To be ashamed to be my father's child! / But though I am a daughter to his blood, / I am not to his manners. O Lorenzo, / If thou keep promise, I shall end this strife, / Become a Christian and thy loving wife.

Oh dear, what a terrible sin it is for me to be ashamed of being my father's child! But though I'm his daughter by blood, I'm not like him in my ways. Oh, Lorenzo, if you keep your promise, I'll end this conflict and become a Christian and your loving wife.
Nay, we will slink away in supper-time, / Disguise us at my lodging, and return / All in an hour.
No, we'll slip away at supper-time, put on our disguises at my lodging and be back, all within an hour.
We have not made good preparation.
We have not spoke us yet of torch-bearers.
We haven't even arranged torch-bearers yet.
'Tis vile, unless it may be quaintly order'd, / And better in my mind not undertook.
It's shabby unless it can be done stylishly, and better, I think, not to do it at all.
'Tis now but four o'clock, we have two hours / To furnish us.
It's only four o'clock. We have two hours to get ready.
And it shall please you to break up this, it shall seem to signify.
If you'd be so kind as to open this, it will seem to signify.
I know the hand, in faith 'tis a fair hand, / And whiter than the paper it writ on / Is the fair hand that writ.
I know the handwriting. Honestly, it's a fine hand, and the beautiful hand that wrote it is whiter than the paper it's written on.
Marry, sir, to bid my old master the Jew to sup tonight with my new / master the Christian.
Why, sir, to invite my old master the Jew to have supper tonight with my new master the Christian.
Hold here, take this. Tell gentle Jessica / I will not fail her, speak it privately. / Go, gentlemen,
Wait, take this. Tell gentle Jessica I won't fail her. Tell her privately. Go. Gentlemen,
Will you prepare you for this masque tonight? / I am provided of a torch-bearer.
will you get ready for this masque tonight? I've found myself a torch-bearer.
Ay, marry, I'll be gone about it straight.
Yes, indeed, I'll go and see to it straight away.
Meet me and Gratiano / At Gratiano's lodging some hour hence.
Meet Gratiano and me at Gratiano's lodging in about an hour.
Was not that letter from fair Jessica?
Wasn't that letter from beautiful Jessica?

I must needs tell thee all. She hath directed / How I shall take her from her father's house, / What gold and jewels she is furnish'd with, / What page's suit she hath in readiness. / If e'er the Jew her father come to heaven, / It will be for his gentle daughter's sake; / And never dare misfortune cross her foot, / Unless she do it under this excuse, / That she is issue to a faithless Jew. / Come, go with me, peruse this as thou goest; / Fair Jessica shall be my torch-bearer.

I'll have to tell you everything. She's told me how I'm to take her from her father's house, what gold and jewels she's taking with her, and what page boy's clothes she has ready. If the Jew her father ever gets to heaven, it'll be thanks to his gentle daughter. And misfortune will never dare to cross her path, unless it uses the excuse that she is the child of an unbelieving Jew. Come with me. Read this as you go. Beautiful Jessica will be my torch-bearer.

Well, thou shalt see, thy eyes shall be thy judge, / The difference of old Shylock and Bassanio.— / What, Jessica!—Thou shalt not gormandize / As thou hast done with me;—What, Jessica!— / And sleep, and snore, and rend apparel out. / Why, Jessica, I say!

Well, you'll see for yourself, your own eyes will judge the difference between old Shylock and Bassanio. Jessica! You won't be able to stuff yourself the way you have with me. Jessica! Or sleep and snore and wear out your clothes. Jessica, I say!
Who bids thee call? I do not bid thee call.
Who told you to call? I didn't tell you to call.
Your worship was wont to tell me I could do nothing without bidding.
Your worship always used to tell me I couldn't do anything without being told.
Call you? What is your will?
Did you call? What do you want?

I am bid forth to supper, Jessica. / There are my keys. But wherefore should I go? / I am not bid for love, they flatter me. / But yet I'll go in hate, to feed upon / The prodigal Christian. Jessica, my girl, / Look to my house. I am right loath to go; / There is some ill a-brewing towards my rest, / For I did dream of money-bags tonight.

I'm invited out to supper, Jessica. Here are my keys. But why should I go? They didn't invite me out of love. They're flattering me. But still, I'll go out of hatred, to eat at the wasteful Christian's expense. Jessica, my girl, look after my house. I really don't want to go. There's some trouble brewing against my peace, because I dreamed of moneybags last night.
I beseech you, sir, go. My young master doth expect your reproach.
Please, sir, go. My young master is expecting your reproach.

And they have conspired together. I will not say you shall see a / masque, but if you do, then it was not for nothing that my nose fell / a-bleeding on Black Monday last at six o'clock i' th' morning, falling / out that year on Ash-Wednesday was four year in th' afternoon.

And they've conspired together. I won't say you'll see a masque, but if you do, then it wasn't for nothing that my nose started bleeding last Easter Monday at six o'clock in the morning, which happened that year on the same day as Ash Wednesday four years ago in the afternoon.

What, are there masques? Hear you me, Jessica, / Lock up my doors, and when you hear the drum / And the vile squealing of the wry-neck'd fife, / Clamber not you up to the casements then, / Nor thrust your head into the public street / To gaze on Christian fools with varnish'd faces, / But stop my house's ears, I mean my casements. / Let not the sound of shallow fopp'ry enter / My sober house. By Jacob's staff I swear / I have no mind of feasting forth tonight. / But I will go. Go you before me, sirrah. / Say I will come.

What, are there going to be masques? Listen to me, Jessica. Lock my doors, and when you hear the drum and the nasty squealing of the crooked fife, don't climb up to the windows or stick your head out into the street to stare at Christian fools with painted faces. Stop up my house's ears, I mean my windows. Don't let the sound of empty foolery get into my sober house. I swear by Jacob's staff, I don't feel like feasting out tonight. But I'll go. You go ahead of me, sir. Say I'll come.
I will go before, sir. / Mistress, look out at window for all this. / There will come a Christian by / Will be worth a Jewess' eye.
I'll go ahead, sir. Mistress, look out of the window anyway. A Christian will come by who'll be worth a Jewish girl's look.
What says that fool of Hagar's offspring, ha?
What's that fool, that son of Hagar, saying, eh?
His words were "Farewell, mistress," nothing else.

The patch is kind enough, but a huge feeder, / Snail-slow in profit, and he sleeps by day / More than the wild-cat. Drones hive not with me, / Therefore I part with him, and part with him / To one that I would have him help to waste / His borrowed purse. Well, Jessica, go in. / Perhaps I will return immediately: / Do as I bid you, shut doors after you, / "Fast bind, fast find." / A proverb never stale in thrifty mind.

The fool is kind enough, but he eats a huge amount, he's as slow as a snail at doing anything useful, and he sleeps in the daytime more than a wildcat. I don't keep drones in my hive, so I'm getting rid of him, and passing him on to someone I'd like him to help waste the money he's borrowed. Well, Jessica, go in. Perhaps I'll come back straight away. Do as I tell you. Shut the doors behind you. "Fast bind, fast find": lock things up tight and you'll find them safe. It's a proverb that never gets old for a careful mind.
Farewell, and if my fortune be not crost, / I have a father, you a daughter, lost.
Goodbye. And if my luck isn't blocked, I've lost a father and you've lost a daughter.
This is the penthouse under which Lorenzo / Desired us to make stand.
This is the porch Lorenzo asked us to wait under.
And it is marvel he out-dwells his hour, / For lovers ever run before the clock.
And it's amazing that he's late, because lovers always run ahead of the clock.
O ten times faster Venus' pigeons fly / To seal love's bonds new-made than they are wont / To keep obliged faith unforfeited!
Oh, Venus's doves fly ten times faster to seal new bonds of love than they do to keep the promises of people already pledged!

That ever holds: who riseth from a feast / With that keen appetite that he sits down? / Where is the horse that doth untread again / His tedious measures with the unbated fire / That he did pace them first? All things that are, / Are with more spirit chased than enjoy'd. / How like a younger or a prodigal / The scarfed bark puts from her native bay, / Hugg'd and embraced by the strumpet wind! / How like the prodigal doth she return / With over-weather'd ribs and ragged sails, / Lean, rent, and beggar'd by the strumpet wind!

That's always true. Who gets up from a feast with as sharp an appetite as when he sat down? Where's the horse that retraces its weary steps with the same undimmed fire it had when it first ran them? Everything that exists is chased with more spirit than it is enjoyed. Look how a ship decked with flags leaves her home port like a younger son or a spendthrift, hugged and embraced by the wind, that whore! And how she comes back like the prodigal son, with weather-beaten timbers and ragged sails, thin, torn and beggared by that whore of a wind!
Here comes Lorenzo, more of this hereafter.
Here comes Lorenzo. More of this later.

Sweet friends, your patience for my long abode. / Not I but my affairs have made you wait. / When you shall please to play the thieves for wives, / I'll watch as long for you then. Approach. / Here dwells my father Jew. Ho! who's within?

Sweet friends, forgive me for being so long. My business made you wait, not me. When you want to play thieves to steal wives, I'll keep watch as long for you. Come here. This is where my Jewish father-in-law lives. Hello! Who's in there?
Who are you? Tell me, for more certainty, / Albeit I'll swear that I do know your tongue.
Who are you? Tell me, to be sure, though I'll swear I know your voice.
Lorenzo certain, and my love indeed, / For who love I so much? And now who knows / But you, Lorenzo, whether I am yours?
Lorenzo certainly, and my love truly, because whom do I love so much? And who but you, Lorenzo, knows whether I'm yours?
Heaven and thy thoughts are witness that thou art.
Heaven and your own thoughts are witnesses that you are.

Here, catch this casket; it is worth the pains. / I am glad 'tis night, you do not look on me, / For I am much asham'd of my exchange. / But love is blind, and lovers cannot see / The pretty follies that themselves commit, / For if they could, Cupid himself would blush / To see me thus transformed to a boy.

Here, catch this box. It's worth the trouble. I'm glad it's night and you can't see me, because I'm very ashamed of my change of clothes. But love is blind, and lovers can't see the pretty follies they commit. If they could, Cupid himself would blush to see me turned into a boy like this.
Descend, for you must be my torch-bearer.
Come down, because you have to be my torch-bearer.
What! must I hold a candle to my shames? / They in themselves, good sooth, are too too light. / Why, 'tis an office of discovery, love, / And I should be obscur'd.
What! Must I hold a candle to my shame? It's already too, too obvious. Why, a torch-bearer's job is to show things up, love, and I ought to be hidden.
So are you, sweet, / Even in the lovely garnish of a boy. / But come at once, / For the close night doth play the runaway, / And we are stay'd for at Bassanio's feast.
And so you are, sweetheart, even in the lovely costume of a boy. But come at once, because the secret night is running away, and they're waiting for us at Bassanio's feast.
I will make fast the doors, and gild myself / With some moe ducats, and be with you straight.
I'll lock the doors, and gild myself with some more ducats, and be with you straight away.
Now, by my hood, a gentle, and no Jew.
Now, by my hood, she's a gentile, not a Jew.

Beshrew me but I love her heartily, / For she is wise, if I can judge of her, / And fair she is, if that mine eyes be true, / And true she is, as she hath prov'd herself. / And therefore, like herself, wise, fair, and true, / Shall she be placed in my constant soul.

Curse me if I don't love her with all my heart. She's wise, if I can judge her, and she's beautiful, if my eyes don't lie, and she's true, as she has proved. So, being what she is, wise, beautiful and true, she'll be kept in my faithful soul.
What, art thou come? On, gentlemen, away! / Our masquing mates by this time for us stay.
What, have you come? On, gentlemen, let's go! Our friends in the masque are waiting for us by now.

Fie, fie, Gratiano! where are all the rest? / 'Tis nine o'clock, our friends all stay for you. / No masque tonight, the wind is come about; / Bassanio presently will go aboard. / I have sent twenty out to seek for you.

Shame on you, Gratiano! Where are all the others? It's nine o'clock. Our friends are all waiting for you. There's no masque tonight. The wind has changed, and Bassanio is going on board at once. I've sent twenty people out to look for you.
I am glad on't. I desire no more delight / Than to be under sail and gone tonight.
I'm glad of it. I want no better fun than to be under sail and away tonight.
Go, draw aside the curtains and discover / The several caskets to this noble prince. / Now make your choice.
Go, draw back the curtains and show the three caskets to this noble prince. Now make your choice.

The first, of gold, who this inscription bears, / "Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire." / The second, silver, which this promise carries, / "Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves." / This third, dull lead, with warning all as blunt, / "Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath." / How shall I know if I do choose the right?

The first, of gold, has this inscription: "Who chooses me shall gain what many men desire." The second, silver, carries this promise: "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." This third, dull lead, has a warning just as blunt: "Who chooses me must give and risk all he has." How will I know if I've chosen right?
The one of them contains my picture, prince. / If you choose that, then I am yours withal.
One of them contains my picture, prince. If you choose that, then I'm yours as well.

Some god direct my judgment! Let me see. / I will survey the inscriptions back again. / What says this leaden casket? / "Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath." / Must give, for what? For lead? Hazard for lead! / This casket threatens; men that hazard all / Do it in hope of fair advantages: / A golden mind stoops not to shows of dross, / I'll then nor give nor hazard aught for lead. / What says the silver with her virgin hue? / "Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves." / As much as he deserves! Pause there, Morocco, / And weigh thy value with an even hand. / If thou be'st rated by thy estimation / Thou dost deserve enough, and yet enough / May not extend so far as to the lady. / And yet to be afeard of my deserving / Were but a weak disabling of myself. / As much as I deserve!
