Why, that's the lady: / I do in birth deserve her, and in fortunes, / In graces, and in qualities of breeding; / But more than these, in love I do deserve. / What if I stray'd no farther, but chose here? / Let's see once more this saying grav'd in gold: / "Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire." / Why, that's the lady, all the world desires her. / From the four corners of the earth they come / To kiss this shrine, this mortal breathing saint. / The Hyrcanian deserts and the vasty wilds / Of wide Arabia are as throughfares now / For princes to come view fair Portia. / The watery kingdom, whose ambitious head / Spets in the face of heaven, is no bar / To stop the foreign spirits, but they come / As o'er a brook to see fair Portia. / One of these three contains her heavenly picture. / Is't like that lead contains her? 'Twere damnation / To think so base a thought. It were too gross / To rib her cerecloth in the obscure grave. / Or shall I think in silver she's immur'd / Being ten times undervalued to tried gold? / O sinful thought! Never so rich a gem / Was set in worse than gold. They have in England / A coin that bears the figure of an angel / Stamped in gold; but that's insculp'd upon; / But here an angel in a golden bed / Lies all within. Deliver me the key. / Here do I choose, and thrive I as I may.

May some god guide my judgment! Let me see. I'll look over the inscriptions again. What does this lead casket say? "Who chooses me must give and risk all he has." Must give, for what? For lead? Risk everything for lead! This casket is threatening. Men who risk everything do it in the hope of a good return. A golden mind doesn't stoop to worthless rubbish. So I won't give or risk anything for lead. What does the silver say, with its pure colour? "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." As much as he deserves! Stop there, Morocco, and weigh your worth fairly. If you're valued by your own reputation, you deserve a great deal, and yet a great deal may not stretch as far as the lady. And yet to be afraid I don't deserve her would be a feeble way of running myself down. As much as I deserve! Why, that's the lady. I deserve her by birth and by wealth, in my graces and my upbringing, but more than these, I deserve her by my love. What if I went no further, and chose here? Let's look once more at this saying carved in gold: "Who chooses me shall gain what many men desire." Why, that's the lady: the whole world desires her. They come from the four corners of the earth to kiss this shrine, this living, breathing saint. The deserts of Persia and the vast wilds of Arabia are highways now for princes coming to see beautiful Portia. The ocean, whose proud waves spit in the face of heaven, is no barrier to stop foreign suitors: they cross it as if it were a stream to see beautiful Portia. One of these three holds her heavenly picture. Is it likely that lead contains her? It would be damnable to think such a low thought. Lead would be too coarse even to wrap her shroud in the dark grave. Or shall I think she's shut up in silver, which is worth ten times less than pure gold? Oh, sinful thought! No gem as rich as this was ever set in anything worse than gold. In England they have a coin with the figure of an angel stamped on it in gold, but that's only engraved on the outside. Here an angel lies inside, in a golden bed. Give me the key. I choose this one, and let me prosper as I may.
There, take it, prince, and if my form lie there, / Then I am yours.
There, take it, prince, and if my picture is in there, then I'm yours.

O hell! what have we here? / A carrion Death, within whose empty eye / There is a written scroll. I'll read the writing. / [Reads] / All that glisters is not gold, / Often have you heard that told. / Many a man his life hath sold / But my outside to behold. / Gilded tombs do worms infold. / Had you been as wise as bold, / Young in limbs, in judgment old, / Your answer had not been inscroll'd, / Fare you well, your suit is cold. / Cold indeed and labour lost, / Then farewell heat, and welcome frost. / Portia, adieu! I have too griev'd a heart / To take a tedious leave. Thus losers part.

Oh, hell! What have we here? A rotting skull, with a written scroll in its empty eye socket. I'll read what it says. [Reads] All that glitters is not gold. You've often heard that said. Many a man has sold his life just to look at my outside. Gilded tombs hold worms. If you had been as wise as you were bold, young in body but old in judgment, you wouldn't have received this written answer. Farewell, your suit has gone cold. Cold indeed, and my effort wasted. Then goodbye, heat, and welcome, frost. Portia, goodbye! My heart is too grieved to make a long farewell. This is how losers leave.
A gentle riddance. Draw the curtains, go. / Let all of his complexion choose me so.
A pleasant riddance. Close the curtains, go. Let everyone of his colour choose like that.
Why, man, I saw Bassanio under sail; / With him is Gratiano gone along; / And in their ship I am sure Lorenzo is not.
Why, man, I saw Bassanio set sail. Gratiano has gone with him. And I'm sure Lorenzo isn't on their ship.
The villain Jew with outcries rais'd the Duke, / Who went with him to search Bassanio's ship.
That villain the Jew woke the Duke with his shouting, and the Duke went with him to search Bassanio's ship.

He came too late, the ship was under sail; / But there the Duke was given to understand / That in a gondola were seen together / Lorenzo and his amorous Jessica. / Besides, Antonio certified the Duke / They were not with Bassanio in his ship.

He came too late. The ship had sailed. But there the Duke was told that Lorenzo and his loving Jessica had been seen together in a gondola. Besides, Antonio assured the Duke they weren't with Bassanio on his ship.

I never heard a passion so confus'd, / So strange, outrageous, and so variable / As the dog Jew did utter in the streets. / "My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter! / Fled with a Christian! O my Christian ducats! / Justice! the law! my ducats and my daughter! / A sealed bag, two sealed bags of ducats, / Of double ducats, stol'n from me by my daughter! / And jewels, two stones, two rich and precious stones, / Stol'n by my daughter! Justice! find the girl, / She hath the stones upon her and the ducats."

I never heard such a confused outburst, so strange, so wild and so changeable, as the one that dog of a Jew let out in the streets. "My daughter! Oh, my ducats! Oh, my daughter! Run off with a Christian! Oh, my Christian ducats! Justice! The law! My ducats and my daughter! A sealed bag, two sealed bags of ducats, of double ducats, stolen from me by my daughter! And jewels, two stones, two rich and precious stones, stolen by my daughter! Justice! Find the girl! She has the stones on her, and the ducats."
Why, all the boys in Venice follow him, / Crying, his stones, his daughter, and his ducats.
Why, all the boys in Venice follow him around, shouting about his stones, his daughter and his ducats.
Let good Antonio look he keep his day / Or he shall pay for this.
Good Antonio had better make sure he pays on the day, or he'll pay for this.

Marry, well rememb'red. / I reason'd with a Frenchman yesterday, / Who told me, in the narrow seas that part / The French and English, there miscarried / A vessel of our country richly fraught. / I thought upon Antonio when he told me, / And wish'd in silence that it were not his.

Yes, that's a good point. I was talking to a Frenchman yesterday who told me that in the Channel, between France and England, a richly loaded ship from our country had been wrecked. I thought of Antonio when he told me, and silently wished it wasn't his.
You were best to tell Antonio what you hear, / Yet do not suddenly, for it may grieve him.
You'd better tell Antonio what you've heard. But don't do it suddenly, because it may upset him.

A kinder gentleman treads not the earth. / I saw Bassanio and Antonio part, / Bassanio told him he would make some speed / Of his return. He answered "Do not so, / Slubber not business for my sake, Bassanio, / But stay the very riping of the time, / And for the Jew's bond which he hath of me, / Let it not enter in your mind of love: / Be merry, and employ your chiefest thoughts / To courtship, and such fair ostents of love / As shall conveniently become you there." / And even there, his eye being big with tears, / Turning his face, he put his hand behind him, / And with affection wondrous sensible / He wrung Bassanio's hand, and so they parted.

There's no kinder gentleman walking the earth. I saw Bassanio and Antonio say goodbye. Bassanio told him he'd hurry back. He answered, "Don't do that. Don't rush your business for my sake, Bassanio. Stay until the time is fully ripe. And as for the Jew's bond that he has from me, don't let it get into your mind, which is full of love. Be happy, and give your main thoughts to courting, and to such fine displays of love as will suit you there." And then, with his eyes full of tears, he turned his face away, put his hand behind him and, with wonderfully deep feeling, squeezed Bassanio's hand. And so they parted.
I think he only loves the world for him. / I pray thee, let us go and find him out / And quicken his embraced heaviness / With some delight or other.
I think he loves the world only for Bassanio's sake. Please, let's go and find him and cheer up the sadness he's holding on to with some pleasure or other.
Quick, quick, I pray thee, draw the curtain straight. / The Prince of Arragon hath ta'en his oath, / And comes to his election presently.
Quick, quick, please, draw the curtain at once. The Prince of Arragon has taken his oath and is coming to make his choice now.

Behold, there stand the caskets, noble Prince, / If you choose that wherein I am contain'd, / Straight shall our nuptial rites be solemniz'd. / But if you fail, without more speech, my lord, / You must be gone from hence immediately.
Look, there are the caskets, noble Prince. If you choose the one I'm in, our wedding will be celebrated at once. But if you fail, my lord, you must leave here immediately without another word.

I am enjoin'd by oath to observe three things: / First, never to unfold to anyone / Which casket 'twas I chose; next, if I fail / Of the right casket, never in my life / To woo a maid in way of marriage; / Lastly, / If I do fail in fortune of my choice, / Immediately to leave you and be gone.

I'm bound by oath to keep three rules. First, never to tell anyone which casket I chose. Next, if I don't pick the right casket, never in my life to court a girl with a view to marriage. Lastly, if I'm unlucky in my choice, to leave you at once and be gone.
To these injunctions everyone doth swear / That comes to hazard for my worthless self.
Everyone who comes to gamble for my worthless self swears to these conditions.

And so have I address'd me. Fortune now / To my heart's hope! Gold, silver, and base lead. / "Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath." / You shall look fairer ere I give or hazard. / What says the golden chest? Ha! let me see: / "Who chooseth me shall gain what many men desire." / What many men desire! that "many" may be meant / By the fool multitude, that choose by show, / Not learning more than the fond eye doth teach, / Which pries not to th' interior, but like the martlet / Builds in the weather on the outward wall, / Even in the force and road of casualty. / I will not choose what many men desire, / Because I will not jump with common spirits / And rank me with the barbarous multitudes. / Why, then to thee, thou silver treasure-house, / Tell me once more what title thou dost bear. / "Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves." / And well said too; for who shall go about / To cozen fortune, and be honourable / Without the stamp of merit? Let none presume / To wear an undeserved dignity. / O that estates, degrees, and offices / Were not deriv'd corruptly, and that clear honour / Were purchas'd by the merit of the wearer! / How many then should cover that stand bare? / How many be commanded that command? / How much low peasantry would then be gleaned / From the true seed of honour? And how much honour / Pick'd from the chaff and ruin of the times, / To be new varnish'd? Well, but to my choice. / "Who chooseth me shall get as much as he deserves." / I will assume desert. Give me a key for this, / And instantly unlock my fortunes here.

And I've prepared myself accordingly. Now, Fortune, answer my heart's hope! Gold, silver and common lead. "Who chooses me must give and risk all he has." You'll have to look better before I give or risk anything. What does the golden chest say? Ha! Let me see. "Who chooses me shall gain what many men desire." What many men desire! That "many" may mean the foolish crowd who choose by appearances, who learn no more than their silly eyes teach them, who don't look inside, but, like the house martin, build their nests outside on the wall, in all weathers, right in the path of danger. I won't choose what many men desire, because I won't go along with common people and rank myself with the uncivilised masses. Why, then, to you, silver treasure house. Tell me once more what label you have. "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." And well said too, because who would try to cheat fortune and be honoured without the stamp of merit? Let no one dare to wear a dignity he doesn't deserve. Oh, if only wealth, rank and high office weren't gained corruptly, and pure honour were earned by the merit of the person who wears it! How many men would then keep their hats on who now stand bare-headed? How many would take orders who now give them? How many low-born peasants would be weeded out from the true seed of honour? And how much honour would be picked out from the rubbish and ruin of the times and polished up again? Well, back to my choice. "Who chooses me shall get as much as he deserves." I'll take it that I deserve. Give me a key for this, and let me unlock my fortune here at once.
Too long a pause for that which you find there.
Too long a pause for what you find there.

What's here? The portrait of a blinking idiot / Presenting me a schedule! I will read it. / How much unlike art thou to Portia! / How much unlike my hopes and my deservings! / "Who chooseth me shall have as much as he deserves." / Did I deserve no more than a fool's head? / Is that my prize? Are my deserts no better?

What's this? A picture of a blinking idiot, handing me a scroll! I'll read it. How unlike Portia you are! How unlike what I hoped for and deserved! "Who chooses me shall have as much as he deserves." Did I deserve no more than a fool's head? Is that my prize? Is that all I'm worth?
To offend and judge are distinct offices, / And of opposed natures.
Committing an offence and judging it are different jobs, and opposites by nature.

What is here? / [Reads] / The fire seven times tried this; / Seven times tried that judgment is / That did never choose amiss. / Some there be that shadows kiss; / Such have but a shadow's bliss. / There be fools alive, I wis, / Silver'd o'er, and so was this. / Take what wife you will to bed, / I will ever be your head: / So be gone; you are sped. / Still more fool I shall appear / By the time I linger here. / With one fool's head I came to woo, / But I go away with two. / Sweet, adieu! I'll keep my oath, / Patiently to bear my wroth.

What's here? [Reads] This silver has been tested seven times in the fire. Judgment that has been tested seven times never chooses wrongly. Some people kiss shadows, and they have only a shadow's happiness. There are fools alive, I know, who are covered in silver, and so was this. Take whatever wife you like to bed, I'll always be your head. So be gone. You're finished. I'll look an even bigger fool the longer I stay here. I came to woo with one fool's head, but I leave with two. Sweetheart, goodbye! I'll keep my oath and bear my grief patiently.
Thus hath the candle sing'd the moth. / O, these deliberate fools! When they do choose, / They have the wisdom by their wit to lose.
So the candle has burned the moth. Oh, these fools who think everything through! When they choose, they're clever enough to lose.
The ancient saying is no heresy: / Hanging and wiving goes by destiny.
The old saying is no lie: hanging and marrying are decided by fate.
Here. What does my lord want?

Madam, there is alighted at your gate / A young Venetian, one that comes before / To signify th' approaching of his lord, / From whom he bringeth sensible regreets; / To wit (besides commends and courteous breath) / Gifts of rich value; yet I have not seen / So likely an ambassador of love. / A day in April never came so sweet, / To show how costly summer was at hand, / As this fore-spurrer comes before his lord.

Madam, a young Venetian has dismounted at your gate. He has come ahead to announce that his lord is on his way, and he brings greetings from him you can touch and see: that is, besides compliments and polite words, rich gifts. I've never seen such a promising messenger of love. No April day ever came so sweetly to show that rich summer was near as this rider comes ahead of his lord.

No more, I pray thee. I am half afeard / Thou wilt say anon he is some kin to thee, / Thou spend'st such high-day wit in praising him. / Come, come, Nerissa, for I long to see / Quick Cupid's post that comes so mannerly.

No more, please. I'm half afraid you'll say next that he's a relative of yours, since you're spending such holiday wit on praising him. Come, come, Nerissa, because I can't wait to see swift Cupid's messenger, who comes so politely.
Bassanio, Lord Love, if thy will it be!
Lord of Love, let it be Bassanio, if it's your will!
Now, what news on the Rialto?
Now, what's the news on the Rialto?

Why, yet it lives there unchecked that Antonio hath a ship of rich / lading wrack'd on the narrow seas; the Goodwins, I think they call the / place, a very dangerous flat and fatal, where the carcasses of many a / tall ship lie buried, as they say, if my gossip Report be an honest / woman of her word.

Why, the rumour is still going round unchallenged that Antonio has had a richly loaded ship wrecked in the Channel. The Goodwins, I think they call the place, a very dangerous and deadly sandbank, where the wrecks of many great ships lie buried, so they say, if old gossip Rumour is an honest woman who keeps her word.

I would she were as lying a gossip in that as ever knapped ginger or / made her neighbours believe she wept for the death of a third husband. / But it is true, without any slips of prolixity or crossing the plain / highway of talk, that the good Antonio, the honest Antonio,—O that I / had a title good enough to keep his name company!—

I wish she were as big a liar about that as any old gossip who ever nibbled ginger or made her neighbours believe she was crying over the death of her third husband. But it's true, without going on about it or straying from the plain road of speech, that the good Antonio, the honest Antonio, oh, if only I had a title good enough to keep his name company!
Come on, get to the full stop.
Ha, what sayest thou? Why, the end is, he hath lost a ship.
What, what are you saying? Why, the end is, he's lost a ship.
I would it might prove the end of his losses.
I wish that would prove the end of his losses.
Let me say "amen" betimes, lest the devil cross my prayer, for here he / comes in the likeness of a Jew.
Let me say "amen" quickly, in case the devil blocks my prayer, because here he comes, looking like a Jew.
How now, Shylock, what news among the merchants?
Well, Shylock, what's the news among the merchants?
You knew, none so well, none so well as you, of my daughter's flight.
You knew, nobody better, nobody better than you, about my daughter running away.
That's certain, I, for my part, knew the tailor that made the wings she / flew withal.
That's for sure. I, for one, knew the tailor who made the wings she flew away with.
And Shylock, for his own part, knew the bird was fledged; and then it / is the complexion of them all to leave the dam.
And Shylock, for his part, knew the bird had her feathers, and it's the nature of all of them to leave their mother then.
That's certain, if the devil may be her judge.
That's certain, if the devil is her judge.
My own flesh and blood to rebel!
My own flesh and blood to rebel!
Out upon it, old carrion! Rebels it at these years?
Shame on you, you old corpse! Does your flesh still rebel at your age?
I say my daughter is my flesh and my blood.
I'm saying my daughter is my flesh and blood.

There is more difference between thy flesh and hers than between jet / and ivory, more between your bloods than there is between red wine and / Rhenish. But tell us, do you hear whether Antonio have had any loss at / sea or no?

There's more difference between your flesh and hers than between black jet and white ivory, and more between your blood and hers than between red wine and white Rhine wine. But tell us, have you heard whether Antonio has had any loss at sea or not?

There I have another bad match, a bankrupt, a prodigal, who dare scarce / show his head on the Rialto, a beggar that used to come so smug upon / the mart; let him look to his bond. He was wont to call me usurer; let / him look to his bond: he was wont to lend money for a Christian cur'sy; / let him look to his bond.

There's another bad deal of mine: a bankrupt, a spendthrift, who hardly dares show his face on the Rialto, a beggar who used to come so smugly to the market. Let him look out for his bond. He used to call me a usurer. Let him look out for his bond. He used to lend money out of Christian courtesy. Let him look out for his bond.
Why, I am sure if he forfeit, thou wilt not take his flesh! What's that / good for?
Why, I'm sure that if he can't pay you won't take his flesh. What good is that?

To bait fish withal; if it will feed nothing else, it will feed my / revenge. He hath disgrac'd me and hind'red me half a million, laugh'd / at my losses, mock'd at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my / bargains, cooled my friends, heated mine enemies. And what's his / reason? I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, / dimensions, senses, affections, passions? Fed with the same food, hurt / with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same / means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian / is? If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not / laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, shall we / not revenge? If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in / that. If a Jew wrong a Christian, what is his humility? Revenge. If a / Christian wrong a Jew, what should his sufferance be by Christian / example? Why, revenge! The villainy you teach me I will execute, and it / shall go hard but I will better the instruction.

To bait fish with. If it'll feed nothing else, it'll feed my revenge. He has disgraced me and cost me half a million, laughed at my losses, mocked my profits, scorned my people, blocked my deals, cooled my friends and stirred up my enemies. And what's his reason? I am a Jew. Hasn't a Jew got eyes? Hasn't a Jew got hands, organs, a body, senses, feelings, passions? Isn't he fed by the same food, hurt by the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same medicines, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is? If you prick us, don't we bleed? If you tickle us, don't we laugh? If you poison us, don't we die? And if you wrong us, shouldn't we take revenge? If we're like you in everything else, we'll be like you in that. If a Jew wrongs a Christian, how does the Christian show his humility? Revenge. If a Christian wrongs a Jew, how should the Jew show patience, following the Christian example? Why, revenge! I'll practise the villainy you teach me, and I'll do my very best to improve on the lesson.
Gentlemen, my master Antonio is at his house, and desires to speak with / you both.
Gentlemen, my master Antonio is at home and would like to speak to you both.
We have been up and down to seek him.
We've been looking for him everywhere.
Here comes another of the tribe; a third cannot be match'd, unless the / devil himself turn Jew.
Here comes another of his tribe. You couldn't find a third to match them, unless the devil himself turned Jew.
How now, Tubal, what news from Genoa? Hast thou found my daughter?
Well, Tubal, what's the news from Genoa? Have you found my daughter?
I often came where I did hear of her, but cannot find her.
I often came to places where I heard about her, but I can't find her.

Why there, there, there, there! A diamond gone cost me two thousand / ducats in Frankfort! The curse never fell upon our nation till now, I / never felt it till now. Two thousand ducats in that, and other / precious, precious jewels. I would my daughter were dead at my foot, / and the jewels in her ear; would she were hearsed at my foot, and the / ducats in her coffin. No news of them? Why so? And I know not what's / spent in the search. Why, thou—loss upon loss! The thief gone with so / much, and so much to find the thief, and no satisfaction, no revenge, / nor no ill luck stirring but what lights o' my shoulders, no sighs but / o' my breathing, no tears but o' my shedding.

Why, there, there, there, there! A diamond gone that cost me two thousand ducats in Frankfurt! The curse never fell on our people until now. I never felt it until now. Two thousand ducats in that, and other precious, precious jewels. I wish my daughter were dead at my feet with the jewels in her ears! I wish she were in her coffin at my feet with the ducats in it! No news of them? Why, no. And I don't know how much has been spent on the search. Why, you, loss on loss! The thief gone with so much, and so much spent to find the thief, and no satisfaction, no revenge, no bad luck around except what lands on my shoulders, no sighs except the ones I breathe, no tears except the ones I shed.
Yes, other men have ill luck too. Antonio, as I heard in Genoa—
Yes, other men have bad luck too. Antonio, as I heard in Genoa—
What, what, what? Ill luck, ill luck?
What, what, what? Bad luck, bad luck?
—hath an argosy cast away coming from Tripolis.
—has lost a merchant ship coming from Tripoli.
I thank God! I thank God! Is it true, is it true?
Thank God! Thank God! Is it true? Is it true?
I spoke with some of the sailors that escaped the wrack.
I spoke to some of the sailors who escaped the wreck.
I thank thee, good Tubal. Good news, good news! Ha, ha, heard in Genoa?
Thank you, good Tubal. Good news, good news! Ha, ha! Heard in Genoa?
Your daughter spent in Genoa, as I heard, one night, fourscore ducats.
Your daughter spent eighty ducats in Genoa in one night, so I heard.
Thou stick'st a dagger in me. I shall never see my gold again. / Fourscore ducats at a sitting! Fourscore ducats!
You're sticking a dagger in me. I'll never see my gold again. Eighty ducats at one go! Eighty ducats!
There came divers of Antonio's creditors in my company to Venice that / swear he cannot choose but break.
Several of Antonio's creditors travelled with me to Venice, and they swear he can't avoid going bankrupt.
I am very glad of it. I'll plague him, I'll torture him. I am glad of / it.
I'm very glad of it. I'll torment him. I'll torture him. I'm glad of it.
One of them showed me a ring that he had of your daughter for a monkey.
One of them showed me a ring your daughter gave him for a monkey.
Out upon her! Thou torturest me, Tubal. It was my turquoise, I had it / of Leah when I was a bachelor. I would not have given it for a / wilderness of monkeys.
Curse her! You're torturing me, Tubal. That was my turquoise. Leah gave it to me before we were married. I wouldn't have given it for a whole wilderness of monkeys.

Nay, that's true, that's very true. Go, Tubal, fee me an officer; / bespeak him a fortnight before. I will have the heart of him if he / forfeit, for were he out of Venice I can make what merchandise I will. / Go, Tubal, and meet me at our synagogue. Go, good Tubal, at our / synagogue, Tubal.

Yes, that's true, that's very true. Go, Tubal, hire me an officer to arrest him. Book him two weeks in advance. I'll have his heart if he fails to pay, because with him out of Venice I can do whatever business I like. Go, Tubal, and meet me at our synagogue. Go, good Tubal. At our synagogue, Tubal.

I pray you tarry, pause a day or two / Before you hazard, for in choosing wrong / I lose your company; therefore forbear a while. / There's something tells me (but it is not love) / I would not lose you, and you know yourself / Hate counsels not in such a quality. / But lest you should not understand me well,— / And yet a maiden hath no tongue but thought,— / I would detain you here some month or two / Before you venture for me. I could teach you / How to choose right, but then I am forsworn. / So will I never be. So may you miss me. / But if you do, you'll make me wish a sin, / That I had been forsworn. Beshrew your eyes, / They have o'erlook'd me and divided me. / One half of me is yours, the other half yours, / Mine own, I would say; but if mine, then yours, / And so all yours. O these naughty times / Puts bars between the owners and their rights! / And so though yours, not yours. Prove it so, / Let Fortune go to hell for it, not I. / I speak too long, but 'tis to peise the time, / To eche it, and to draw it out in length, / To stay you from election.

Please wait, pause for a day or two before you take your chance, because if you choose wrong I lose your company. So hold back a while. Something tells me, though it isn't love, that I don't want to lose you, and you know yourself that hatred doesn't give advice like this. But in case you don't understand me properly, and a young woman can only think, not speak, her feelings, I'd like to keep you here for a month or two before you gamble for me. I could teach you how to choose right, but then I'd be breaking my oath. I'll never do that. So you may fail to win me. But if you do, you'll make me wish I'd sinned and broken my oath. Curse your eyes! They've bewitched me and split me in two. One half of me is yours, the other half yours, my own, I mean, but if it's mine, then it's yours, and so all of me is yours. Oh, these wicked times put barriers between owners and what belongs to them! And so, though I'm yours, I'm not yours. If it turns out like that, let Fortune go to hell for it, not me. I'm talking too long, but it's to weigh down the time, to stretch it and draw it out, to keep you from choosing.
Let me choose, / For as I am, I live upon the rack.
Let me choose, because as things are, I'm living on the torturer's rack.
Upon the rack, Bassanio! Then confess / What treason there is mingled with your love.
On the rack, Bassanio! Then confess what treason is mixed with your love.
None but that ugly treason of mistrust, / Which makes me fear th' enjoying of my love. / There may as well be amity and life / 'Tween snow and fire as treason and my love.
None except that ugly treason of doubt, which makes me afraid I won't get to enjoy my love. There could as easily be friendship and life between snow and fire as treason in my love.
Ay, but I fear you speak upon the rack / Where men enforced do speak anything.
Yes, but I'm afraid you're speaking on the rack, where men under torture will say anything.
Promise me life, and I'll confess the truth.
Promise me my life, and I'll confess the truth.
"Confess and love" / Had been the very sum of my confession: / O happy torment, when my torturer / Doth teach me answers for deliverance! / But let me to my fortune and the caskets.
"Confess and love" would have been the whole of my confession. Oh, happy torture, when my torturer teaches me the answers that will set me free! But let me go to my fortune and the caskets.

Away, then! I am lock'd in one of them. / If you do love me, you will find me out. / Nerissa and the rest, stand all aloof. / Let music sound while he doth make his choice. / Then if he lose he makes a swan-like end, / Fading in music. That the comparison / May stand more proper, my eye shall be the stream / And wat'ry death-bed for him. He may win, / And what is music then? Then music is / Even as the flourish when true subjects bow / To a new-crowned monarch. Such it is / As are those dulcet sounds in break of day / That creep into the dreaming bridegroom's ear / And summon him to marriage. Now he goes, / With no less presence, but with much more love / Than young Alcides when he did redeem / The virgin tribute paid by howling Troy / To the sea-monster: I stand for sacrifice; / The rest aloof are the Dardanian wives, / With bleared visages come forth to view / The issue of th' exploit. Go, Hercules! / Live thou, I live. With much much more dismay / I view the fight than thou that mak'st the fray.

Go on, then! I'm locked in one of them. If you love me, you'll find me. Nerissa and the rest of you, all stand back. Let music play while he makes his choice. Then if he loses, he'll die like the swan, fading away in music. And to make the comparison more fitting, my eyes will be the stream and his watery deathbed. He may win, and what is the music then? Then the music is like the fanfare when loyal subjects bow to a newly crowned king. It's like those sweet sounds at daybreak that creep into the dreaming bridegroom's ear and call him to his wedding. Now he goes, with no less dignity but much more love than young Hercules had when he rescued the young woman whom wailing Troy was paying as tribute to the sea monster. I am the sacrifice. The others standing back are the Trojan wives, come out with tear-stained faces to see how the adventure turns out. Go, Hercules! If you live, I live. I watch the fight with much, much more fear than you who are fighting it.

[Sings] / Tell me where is fancy bred, / Or in the heart or in the head? / How begot, how nourished? / Reply, reply. / It is engend'red in the eyes, / With gazing fed, and fancy dies / In the cradle where it lies. / Let us all ring fancy's knell: / I'll begin it.—Ding, dong, bell.

[Sings] Tell me where desire is born, in the heart or in the head? How is it conceived, how is it fed? Answer, answer. It is born in the eyes, fed by gazing, and desire dies in the cradle where it lies. Let's all ring desire's funeral bell. I'll start it: ding, dong, bell.

So may the outward shows be least themselves. / The world is still deceiv'd with ornament. / In law, what plea so tainted and corrupt / But, being season'd with a gracious voice, / Obscures the show of evil? In religion, / What damned error but some sober brow / Will bless it, and approve it with a text, / Hiding the grossness with fair ornament? / There is no vice so simple but assumes / Some mark of virtue on his outward parts. / How many cowards, whose hearts are all as false / As stairs of sand, wear yet upon their chins / The beards of Hercules and frowning Mars, / Who inward search'd, have livers white as milk, / And these assume but valour's excrement / To render them redoubted. Look on beauty, / And you shall see 'tis purchas'd by the weight, / Which therein works a miracle in nature, / Making them lightest that wear most of it: / So are those crisped snaky golden locks / Which make such wanton gambols with the wind / Upon supposed fairness, often known / To be the dowry of a second head, / The skull that bred them in the sepulchre. / Thus ornament is but the guiled shore / To a most dangerous sea; the beauteous scarf / Veiling an Indian beauty; in a word, / The seeming truth which cunning times put on / To entrap the wisest. Therefore thou gaudy gold, / Hard food for Midas, I will none of thee, / Nor none of thee, thou pale and common drudge / 'Tween man and man: but thou, thou meagre lead, / Which rather threaten'st than dost promise aught, / Thy palenness moves me more than eloquence, / And here choose I, joy be the consequence!

So the outside may be least like what is inside. The world is always fooled by decoration. In law, what case is so rotten and corrupt that, flavoured with a pleasing voice, it doesn't hide the look of evil? In religion, what damnable error is there that some serious-looking man won't bless and support with a Bible verse, hiding its ugliness with fine decoration? There's no vice so simple that it doesn't put on some outward sign of virtue. How many cowards, whose hearts are as unreliable as stairs made of sand, still wear on their chins the beards of Hercules and frowning Mars, though inside they have livers as white as milk? They put on courage's outgrowth, a beard, only to make people fear them. Look at beauty, and you'll see it's bought by the ounce, in cosmetics, which works a miracle of nature: it makes the women who wear most of it the lightest in morals. It's the same with those curly golden locks that play so flirtatiously with the wind on a woman thought to be beautiful. They often turn out to be a wig, a gift from a second head, the dead woman whose skull grew them, now in the grave. So decoration is just the treacherous shore of a very dangerous sea, the beautiful veil hiding a dark-skinned Indian beauty. In a word, it's the false appearance of truth that these crafty times put on to trap the wisest people. So, you showy gold, hard food for Midas, I'll have none of you. Nor of you, you pale, common drudge passed from hand to hand. But you, you meagre lead, which threaten more than you promise anything, your plainness moves me more than eloquence, and I choose here. Let joy be the result!

[Aside] How all the other passions fleet to air, / As doubtful thoughts, and rash-embrac'd despair, / And shudd'ring fear, and green-ey'd jealousy. / O love, be moderate; allay thy ecstasy, / In measure rain thy joy; scant this excess! / I feel too much thy blessing, make it less, / For fear I surfeit.

[Aside] How all my other feelings vanish into air: anxious thoughts, despair too quickly embraced, shuddering fear and green-eyed jealousy! Oh, love, be moderate. Calm your ecstasy, rain your joy down in measure, cut back this excess! I feel your blessing too much. Make it less, in case I'm overwhelmed.

What find I here? [Opening the leaden casket] / Fair Portia's counterfeit! What demi-god / Hath come so near creation? Move these eyes? / Or whether, riding on the balls of mine, / Seem they in motion? Here are sever'd lips, / Parted with sugar breath, so sweet a bar / Should sunder such sweet friends. Here in her hairs / The painter plays the spider, and hath woven / A golden mesh t'entrap the hearts of men / Faster than gnats in cobwebs. But her eyes!— / How could he see to do them? Having made one, / Methinks it should have power to steal both his / And leave itself unfurnish'd. Yet look how far / The substance of my praise doth wrong this shadow / In underprizing it, so far this shadow / Doth limp behind the substance. Here's the scroll, / The continent and summary of my fortune. / [Reads] / You that choose not by the view / Chance as fair and choose as true! / Since this fortune falls to you, / Be content and seek no new. / If you be well pleas'd with this, / And hold your fortune for your bliss, / Turn to where your lady is, / And claim her with a loving kiss. / A gentle scroll. Fair lady, by your leave, [Kissing her] / I come by note to give and to receive. / Like one of two contending in a prize / That thinks he hath done well in people's eyes, / Hearing applause and universal shout, / Giddy in spirit, still gazing in a doubt / Whether those peals of praise be his or no, / So, thrice-fair lady, stand I even so, / As doubtful whether what I see be true, / Until confirm'd, sign'd, ratified by you.

What do I find here? [Opening the leaden casket] Beautiful Portia's portrait! What half-god of a painter has come so close to creating life? Do these eyes move? Or do they only seem to move because they're riding on my own eyeballs? Here are parted lips, parted by sweet breath, which is the only barrier sweet enough to separate such sweet friends. Here in her hair the painter has played the spider, and woven a golden net to trap men's hearts more firmly than gnats in cobwebs. But her eyes! How could he see to paint them? Once he had painted one, I'd have thought it would have the power to steal both of his and leave itself without a partner. But look: just as my praise does this painted shadow wrong by undervaluing it, so this shadow limps far behind the real woman. Here's the scroll, which contains and sums up my fortune. [Reads] You who don't choose by appearances, you're lucky and you choose rightly! Since this fortune has come to you, be content and look for no other. If you're happy with this and think your fortune your joy, turn to where your lady is and claim her with a loving kiss. A kind scroll. Beautiful lady, with your permission, [Kissing her] I come as the note tells me, to give and to receive. Like one of two competitors for a prize who thinks he has done well in the crowd's eyes, and hearing the applause and the shouting is dizzy with excitement, still staring and doubting whether those roars of praise are for him or not, that's how I stand, three times beautiful lady, unsure whether what I see is true until you confirm it, sign it and approve it.

You see me, Lord Bassanio, where I stand, / Such as I am; though for myself alone / I would not be ambitious in my wish / To wish myself much better, yet for you / I would be trebled twenty times myself, / A thousand times more fair, ten thousand times / More rich, / That only to stand high in your account, / I might in virtues, beauties, livings, friends, / Exceed account. But the full sum of me / Is sum of something, which, to term in gross, / Is an unlesson'd girl, unschool'd, unpractis'd; / Happy in this, she is not yet so old / But she may learn; happier than this, / She is not bred so dull but she can learn; / Happiest of all, is that her gentle spirit / Commits itself to yours to be directed, / As from her lord, her governor, her king. / Myself, and what is mine, to you and yours / Is now converted. But now I was the lord / Of this fair mansion, master of my servants, / Queen o'er myself; and even now, but now, / This house, these servants, and this same myself / Are yours,—my lord's. I give them with this ring, / Which when you part from, lose, or give away, / Let it presage the ruin of your love, / And be my vantage to exclaim on you.

You see me, Lord Bassanio, where I stand, just as I am. Though for myself alone I wouldn't be ambitious enough to wish to be much better, for you I'd like to be twenty times three times better than I am, a thousand times more beautiful, ten thousand times richer, so that, just to rate highly in your eyes, I might have more virtues, beauty, wealth and friends than anyone could count. But the full sum of me adds up to something which, in total, is an unlearned girl, unschooled and inexperienced. She's lucky in this: she isn't so old that she can't learn. Luckier still, she isn't so stupid that she can't learn. Luckiest of all, her gentle spirit gives itself to yours to be guided, as by her lord, her governor, her king. I and everything I own are now turned into you and yours. A moment ago I was the lord of this beautiful house, master of my servants, queen over myself. And now, this very moment, this house, these servants and this same self of mine are yours, my lord's. I give them with this ring. If you ever part with it, lose it or give it away, let that foretell the end of your love, and give me the right to accuse you.

Madam, you have bereft me of all words, / Only my blood speaks to you in my veins, / And there is such confusion in my powers / As after some oration fairly spoke / By a beloved prince, there doth appear / Among the buzzing pleased multitude, / Where every something being blent together, / Turns to a wild of nothing, save of joy / Express'd and not express'd. But when this ring / Parts from this finger, then parts life from hence. / O then be bold to say Bassanio's dead!

Madam, you've robbed me of all words. Only my blood speaks to you in my veins, and my senses are in such confusion, like the buzzing of a pleased crowd after a fine speech by a beloved prince, where every sound blends together into a wilderness of nothing except joy, spoken and unspoken. But when this ring leaves this finger, then life will have left this body. Oh, then you can be sure Bassanio's dead!
My lord and lady, it is now our time, / That have stood by and seen our wishes prosper, / To cry, good joy. Good joy, my lord and lady!
My lord and lady, it's now time for those of us who have stood by and seen our wishes come true to shout, "Joy to you!" Joy to you, my lord and lady!

My Lord Bassanio, and my gentle lady, / I wish you all the joy that you can wish; / For I am sure you can wish none from me. / And when your honours mean to solemnize / The bargain of your faith, I do beseech you / Even at that time I may be married too.

My Lord Bassanio, and my gentle lady, I wish you all the joy you can wish for, because I'm sure you won't wish any away from me. And when you plan to celebrate the agreement of your marriage, I beg you to let me be married at the same time.
With all my heart, so thou canst get a wife.
With all my heart, if you can get a wife.

I thank your lordship, you have got me one. / My eyes, my lord, can look as swift as yours: / You saw the mistress, I beheld the maid. / You lov'd, I lov'd; for intermission / No more pertains to me, my lord, than you. / Your fortune stood upon the caskets there, / And so did mine too, as the matter falls. / For wooing here until I sweat again, / And swearing till my very roof was dry / With oaths of love, at last, (if promise last) / I got a promise of this fair one here / To have her love, provided that your fortune / Achiev'd her mistress.

Thank you, my lord, you've got me one. My eyes, my lord, can look as quickly as yours. You saw the mistress, I saw the maid. You loved, I loved, because I don't like waiting any more than you do, my lord. Your fortune depended on the caskets there, and as it turns out, so did mine. Because after wooing here until I sweated, and swearing oaths of love until the roof of my mouth was dry, I finally got a promise, if promises last, from this beauty here, that she'd love me, provided you were lucky enough to win her mistress.
Madam, it is, so you stand pleas'd withal.
It is, madam, if you're happy with it.
And do you, Gratiano, mean good faith?
And do you mean it seriously, Gratiano?
Our feast shall be much honoured in your marriage.
Your marriage will do our wedding feast great honour.
We'll play with them the first boy for a thousand ducats.
We'll bet them a thousand ducats on which couple has the first boy.
What! And put the stake down now?
No, we shall ne'er win at that sport and stake down. / But who comes here? Lorenzo and his infidel? / What, and my old Venetian friend, Salerio!
No, we'll never win at that game with the stake down. But who's this coming? Lorenzo and his unbeliever? What, and my old Venetian friend Salerio!
Lorenzo and Salerio, welcome hither, / If that the youth of my new int'rest here / Have power to bid you welcome. By your leave, / I bid my very friends and countrymen, / Sweet Portia, welcome.
Lorenzo and Salerio, welcome here, if someone so newly in charge here has the right to welcome you. With your permission, sweet Portia, I welcome my true friends and fellow countrymen.
So do I, my lord, / They are entirely welcome.
So do I, my lord. They're entirely welcome.
I thank your honour. For my part, my lord, / My purpose was not to have seen you here, / But meeting with Salerio by the way, / He did entreat me, past all saying nay, / To come with him along.
Thank you, my lord. For my part, my lord, I didn't plan to see you here, but I met Salerio on the way and he begged me, so that I couldn't say no, to come along with him.
I did, my lord, / And I have reason for it. Signior Antonio / Commends him to you.
I did, my lord, and I have a reason. Signior Antonio sends his regards.
Ere I ope his letter, / I pray you tell me how my good friend doth.
Before I open his letter, please tell me how my good friend is.
Not sick, my lord, unless it be in mind, / Nor well, unless in mind. His letter there / Will show you his estate.
He isn't ill, my lord, unless it's in his mind, and he isn't well, except in his mind. His letter there will show you how things stand with him.

Nerissa, cheer yond stranger, bid her welcome. / Your hand, Salerio. What's the news from Venice? / How doth that royal merchant, good Antonio? / I know he will be glad of our success. / We are the Jasons, we have won the fleece.

Nerissa, cheer up that stranger, make her welcome. Your hand, Salerio. What's the news from Venice? How is that royal merchant, good Antonio? I know he'll be glad of our success. We're the Jasons, we've won the golden fleece.
I would you had won the fleece that he hath lost.
I wish you'd won the fleet he's lost.

There are some shrewd contents in yond same paper / That steals the colour from Bassanio's cheek. / Some dear friend dead, else nothing in the world / Could turn so much the constitution / Of any constant man. What, worse and worse? / With leave, Bassanio, I am half yourself, / And I must freely have the half of anything / That this same paper brings you.

There's some bad news in that paper, stealing the colour from Bassanio's cheek. Some dear friend must be dead. Nothing else in the world could change a steady man so much. What, worse and worse? Forgive me, Bassanio, I'm half of you, and I must freely have half of anything this paper brings you.

O sweet Portia, / Here are a few of the unpleasant'st words / That ever blotted paper. Gentle lady, / When I did first impart my love to you, / I freely told you all the wealth I had / Ran in my veins, I was a gentleman. / And then I told you true. And yet, dear lady, / Rating myself at nothing, you shall see / How much I was a braggart. When I told you / My state was nothing, I should then have told you / That I was worse than nothing; for indeed / I have engag'd myself to a dear friend, / Engag'd my friend to his mere enemy, / To feed my means. Here is a letter, lady, / The paper as the body of my friend, / And every word in it a gaping wound / Issuing life-blood. But is it true, Salerio? / Hath all his ventures fail'd? What, not one hit? / From Tripolis, from Mexico, and England, / From Lisbon, Barbary, and India, / And not one vessel scape the dreadful touch / Of merchant-marring rocks?

Oh, sweet Portia, here are some of the most unpleasant words that ever blotted paper. Gentle lady, when I first told you of my love, I freely told you that all the wealth I had ran in my veins: I was a gentleman. And I told you the truth. And yet, dear lady, when I rated myself as worth nothing, you'll see what a boaster I was. When I told you I had nothing, I should have told you I was worse than nothing, because in fact I've put myself in debt to a dear friend, and put my friend in debt to his deadly enemy, to provide for myself. Here is a letter, lady. The paper is like my friend's body, and every word in it is a gaping wound pouring out his lifeblood. But is it true, Salerio? Have all his ventures failed? What, not one success? From Tripoli, from Mexico and England, from Lisbon, North Africa and India, and not one ship escaped the terrible touch of the rocks that ruin merchants?

Not one, my lord. / Besides, it should appear, that if he had / The present money to discharge the Jew, / He would not take it. Never did I know / A creature that did bear the shape of man / So keen and greedy to confound a man. / He plies the Duke at morning and at night, / And doth impeach the freedom of the state / If they deny him justice. Twenty merchants, / The Duke himself, and the magnificoes / Of greatest port have all persuaded with him, / But none can drive him from the envious plea / Of forfeiture, of justice, and his bond.

Not one, my lord. Besides, it seems that even if he had the cash now to pay off the Jew, the Jew wouldn't take it. I never knew a creature in human shape so keen and greedy to destroy a man. He pesters the Duke morning and night, and says it calls the city's freedom into question if they deny him justice. Twenty merchants, the Duke himself and the most important noblemen have all tried to persuade him, but nobody can drive him away from his malicious demand for the penalty, for justice and for his bond.

When I was with him, I have heard him swear / To Tubal and to Chus, his countrymen, / That he would rather have Antonio's flesh / Than twenty times the value of the sum / That he did owe him. And I know, my lord, / If law, authority, and power deny not, / It will go hard with poor Antonio.

When I was with him, I heard him swear to Tubal and Chus, his countrymen, that he would rather have Antonio's flesh than twenty times the sum Antonio owed him. And I know, my lord, that unless law, authority and power stop him, it will go badly for poor Antonio.
Is it your dear friend that is thus in trouble?
Is it your dear friend who's in this trouble?

The dearest friend to me, the kindest man, / The best condition'd and unwearied spirit / In doing courtesies, and one in whom / The ancient Roman honour more appears / Than any that draws breath in Italy.
The dearest friend I have, the kindest man, the best-natured and most tireless in doing good turns, and a man in whom the honour of ancient Rome shows more than in anyone alive in Italy.
What sum owes he the Jew?
How much does he owe the Jew?

What, no more? / Pay him six thousand, and deface the bond. / Double six thousand, and then treble that, / Before a friend of this description / Shall lose a hair through Bassanio's fault. / First go with me to church and call me wife, / And then away to Venice to your friend. / For never shall you lie by Portia's side / With an unquiet soul. You shall have gold / To pay the petty debt twenty times over. / When it is paid, bring your true friend along. / My maid Nerissa and myself meantime, / Will live as maids and widows. Come, away! / For you shall hence upon your wedding day. / Bid your friends welcome, show a merry cheer; / Since you are dear bought, I will love you dear. / But let me hear the letter of your friend.

What, no more? Pay him six thousand and tear up the bond. Double six thousand, and then triple that, before a friend like that loses a single hair through Bassanio's fault. First come to church with me and make me your wife, and then go to Venice to your friend. You will never lie at Portia's side with a troubled soul. You'll have gold to pay the little debt twenty times over. When it's paid, bring your true friend back with you. Meanwhile my maid Nerissa and I will live like virgins and widows. Come, let's go! You must leave on your wedding day. Welcome your friends and look cheerful. Since you cost me so much, I'll love you dearly. But let me hear your friend's letter.

Sweet Bassanio, my ships have all miscarried, my creditors grow cruel, / my estate is very low, my bond to the Jew is forfeit, and since in / paying it, it is impossible I should live, all debts are clear'd / between you and I, if I might but see you at my death. Notwithstanding, / use your pleasure. If your love do not persuade you to come, let not my / letter.

Sweet Bassanio, my ships have all been lost, my creditors are getting cruel, my wealth is very low, my bond to the Jew is forfeit, and since it is impossible for me to live once I've paid it, all debts between you and me are cleared, if only I could see you before I die. All the same, do as you wish. If your love doesn't persuade you to come, don't let my letter.
O love, dispatch all business and be gone!
Oh, my love, finish all your business and go!
Since I have your good leave to go away, / I will make haste; but, till I come again, / No bed shall e'er be guilty of my stay, / Nor rest be interposer 'twixt us twain.
Since I have your kind permission to go, I'll hurry. But until I come back, no bed will be to blame for keeping me away, and no rest will come between the two of us.
Gaoler, look to him. Tell not me of mercy. / This is the fool that lent out money gratis. / Gaoler, look to him.
Jailer, keep an eye on him. Don't talk to me about mercy. This is the fool who lent out money free of charge. Jailer, keep an eye on him.

I'll have my bond, speak not against my bond. / I have sworn an oath that I will have my bond. / Thou call'dst me dog before thou hadst a cause, / But since I am a dog, beware my fangs; / The Duke shall grant me justice. I do wonder, / Thou naughty gaoler, that thou art so fond / To come abroad with him at his request.

I'll have my bond. Don't speak against my bond. I've sworn an oath that I'll have my bond. You called me dog before you had any reason to, but since I'm a dog, beware my fangs. The Duke will grant me justice. I'm amazed, you useless jailer, that you're foolish enough to bring him out at his request.
I pray thee hear me speak.

I'll have my bond. I will not hear thee speak. / I'll have my bond, and therefore speak no more. / I'll not be made a soft and dull-eyed fool, / To shake the head, relent, and sigh, and yield / To Christian intercessors. Follow not, / I'll have no speaking, I will have my bond.

I'll have my bond. I won't hear you speak. I'll have my bond, so say no more. I won't be turned into a soft, dim-eyed fool who shakes his head, relents, sighs and gives in to Christians pleading for him. Don't follow me. I'll have no talking. I'll have my bond.
It is the most impenetrable cur / That ever kept with men.
He's the most stubborn dog that ever lived among men.

Let him alone. / I'll follow him no more with bootless prayers. / He seeks my life, his reason well I know: / I oft deliver'd from his forfeitures / Many that have at times made moan to me. / Therefore he hates me.

Leave him alone. I won't follow him any more with useless pleading. He wants my life, and I know his reason well: I've often rescued people from his penalties when they came to me complaining. That's why he hates me.
I am sure the Duke / Will never grant this forfeiture to hold.
I'm sure the Duke will never allow this penalty to stand.

The Duke cannot deny the course of law, / For the commodity that strangers have / With us in Venice, if it be denied, / 'Twill much impeach the justice of the state, / Since that the trade and profit of the city / Consisteth of all nations. Therefore, go. / These griefs and losses have so bated me / That I shall hardly spare a pound of flesh / Tomorrow to my bloody creditor. / Well, gaoler, on, pray God Bassanio come / To see me pay his debt, and then I care not.

The Duke can't stop the law taking its course, because if the rights that foreigners enjoy with us in Venice are denied, it will badly damage the justice of the state, since the city's trade and profit depend on all nations. So, go. These griefs and losses have worn me down so much that I'll hardly have a pound of flesh to spare tomorrow for my bloodthirsty creditor. Well, jailer, lead on. I pray to God that Bassanio comes to see me pay his debt, and then I don't care.

Madam, although I speak it in your presence, / You have a noble and a true conceit / Of godlike amity, which appears most strongly / In bearing thus the absence of your lord. / But if you knew to whom you show this honour, / How true a gentleman you send relief, / How dear a lover of my lord your husband, / I know you would be prouder of the work / Than customary bounty can enforce you.

Madam, though I say it to your face, you have a noble and true understanding of godlike friendship, which shows most strongly in the way you bear your husband's absence. But if you knew whom you're honouring like this, what a true gentleman you're sending help to, how dear a friend he is to my lord your husband, I know you'd be prouder of this good deed than your usual generosity could make you.

I never did repent for doing good, / Nor shall not now; for in companions / That do converse and waste the time together, / Whose souls do bear an equal yoke of love, / There must be needs a like proportion / Of lineaments, of manners, and of spirit; / Which makes me think that this Antonio, / Being the bosom lover of my lord, / Must needs be like my lord. If it be so, / How little is the cost I have bestowed / In purchasing the semblance of my soul / From out the state of hellish cruelty! / This comes too near the praising of myself; / Therefore no more of it. Hear other things. / Lorenzo, I commit into your hands / The husbandry and manage of my house / Until my lord's return. For mine own part, / I have toward heaven breath'd a secret vow / To live in prayer and contemplation, / Only attended by Nerissa here, / Until her husband and my lord's return. / There is a monastery two miles off, / And there we will abide. I do desire you / Not to deny this imposition, / The which my love and some necessity / Now lays upon you.

I've never regretted doing good, and I won't now. Friends who talk and spend their time together, and whose souls share love equally, like a pair of oxen sharing a yoke, must be alike in their looks, their manners and their spirit. That makes me think that this Antonio, being my husband's closest friend, must be like my husband. If so, how little I've spent to rescue the likeness of my own soul from a state of hellish cruelty! This is getting too close to praising myself, so no more of it. Listen to other things. Lorenzo, I'm putting the running and management of my house into your hands until my husband comes back. For my part, I've made a secret vow to heaven to live in prayer and contemplation, with only Nerissa here for company, until her husband and mine return. There's a monastery two miles away, and we'll stay there. Please don't refuse this task, which my love and some necessity now put on you.
Madam, with all my heart / I shall obey you in all fair commands.
Madam, I'll obey all your fair commands with all my heart.
My people do already know my mind, / And will acknowledge you and Jessica / In place of Lord Bassanio and myself. / So fare you well till we shall meet again.
My household already knows what I want, and they'll treat you and Jessica in place of Lord Bassanio and me. So goodbye until we meet again.
Fair thoughts and happy hours attend on you!
May happy thoughts and happy hours go with you!
I wish your ladyship all heart's content.
I wish your ladyship everything your heart desires.
I thank you for your wish, and am well pleas'd / To wish it back on you. Fare you well, Jessica.
Thank you for your wish, and I'm happy to wish the same back to you. Goodbye, Jessica.

Now, Balthazar, / As I have ever found thee honest-true, / So let me find thee still. Take this same letter, / And use thou all th' endeavour of a man / In speed to Padua, see thou render this / Into my cousin's hands, Doctor Bellario; / And look what notes and garments he doth give thee, / Bring them, I pray thee, with imagin'd speed / Unto the traject, to the common ferry / Which trades to Venice. Waste no time in words, / But get thee gone. I shall be there before thee.

Now, Balthazar, I've always found you honest and loyal, so let me find you so still. Take this letter, and go as fast as any man can to Padua. Make sure you put it into the hands of my cousin, Doctor Bellario. And whatever papers and clothes he gives you, please bring them as fast as you can imagine to the ferry landing, the public ferry that goes to Venice. Don't waste time talking, just go. I'll be there before you.
Madam, I go with all convenient speed.
Madam, I'll go as fast as I can.
Come on, Nerissa, I have work in hand / That you yet know not of; we'll see our husbands / Before they think of us.
Come on, Nerissa. I'm working on a plan you don't know about yet. We'll see our husbands before they think of us.

They shall, Nerissa, but in such a habit / That they shall think we are accomplished / With that we lack. I'll hold thee any wager, / When we are both accoutered like young men, / I'll prove the prettier fellow of the two, / And wear my dagger with the braver grace, / And speak between the change of man and boy / With a reed voice; and turn two mincing steps / Into a manly stride; and speak of frays / Like a fine bragging youth; and tell quaint lies / How honourable ladies sought my love, / Which I denying, they fell sick and died; / I could not do withal. Then I'll repent, / And wish for all that, that I had not kill'd them. / And twenty of these puny lies I'll tell, / That men shall swear I have discontinued school / About a twelvemonth. I have within my mind / A thousand raw tricks of these bragging Jacks, / Which I will practise.

They will, Nerissa, but dressed in such a way that they'll think we have what we lack. I'll bet you anything that when we're both dressed up as young men, I'll turn out the prettier fellow of the two, and wear my dagger with the more swaggering style, and speak in a squeaky voice, like a boy whose voice is breaking, and turn two dainty steps into one manly stride, and talk about fights like a fine bragging youth, and tell clever lies about how honourable ladies wanted my love, and when I refused them they fell ill and died, and I couldn't help it. Then I'll be sorry, and wish, all the same, that I hadn't killed them. I'll tell twenty of these little lies, so that men will swear I left school a year ago. I have in my head a thousand crude tricks of these bragging lads, and I'll practise them.
Why, shall we turn to men?
Why, are we going to turn into men?

Fie, what a question's that, / If thou wert near a lewd interpreter! / But come, I'll tell thee all my whole device / When I am in my coach, which stays for us / At the park gate; and therefore haste away, / For we must measure twenty miles today.

Shame on you, what a question, if anyone with a dirty mind were nearby to take it the wrong way! But come, I'll tell you my whole plan when we're in my coach, which is waiting for us at the park gate. So hurry, because we have to cover twenty miles today.

Yes, truly, for look you, the sins of the father are to be laid upon / the children, therefore, I promise you, I fear you. I was always plain / with you, and so now I speak my agitation of the matter. Therefore be / of good cheer, for truly I think you are damn'd. There is but one hope / in it that can do you any good, and that is but a kind of bastard hope / neither.

Yes, really, because, you see, the sins of the father are to be punished in the children. So, I promise you, I'm afraid for you. I was always plain with you, and so now I'm telling you my agitation on the subject. So cheer up, because I really think you're damned. There's only one hope that can do you any good, and that's a kind of bastard hope anyway.
And what hope is that, I pray thee?
And what hope is that, please?
Marry, you may partly hope that your father got you not, that you are / not the Jew's daughter.
Well, you can partly hope your father didn't father you, and that you aren't the Jew's daughter.
That were a kind of bastard hope indeed; so the sins of my mother / should be visited upon me.
That would be a bastard hope indeed. Then I'd be punished for my mother's sins.
Truly then I fear you are damn'd both by father and mother; thus when I / shun Scylla your father, I fall into Charybdis your mother. Well, you / are gone both ways.
Truly, then, I'm afraid you're damned by both father and mother. So when I avoid Scylla, your father, I fall into Charybdis, your mother. Well, you're lost either way.
I shall be saved by my husband. He hath made me a Christian.
I'll be saved by my husband. He has made me a Christian.

Truly the more to blame he, we were Christians enow before, e'en as / many as could well live one by another. This making of Christians will / raise the price of hogs; if we grow all to be pork-eaters, we shall not / shortly have a rasher on the coals for money.

Then he's all the more to blame. There were enough Christians before, just as many as could live alongside each other. This making of Christians will raise the price of pigs. If we all become pork-eaters, soon we won't be able to get a rasher of bacon on the fire for any money.
I'll tell my husband, Launcelet, what you say. Here he comes.
I'll tell my husband what you're saying, Launcelet. Here he comes.
I shall grow jealous of you shortly, Launcelet, if you thus get my wife / into corners!
I'll get jealous of you soon, Launcelet, if you keep getting my wife into corners like this!

Nay, you need not fear us, Lorenzo. Launcelet and I are out. He tells / me flatly there's no mercy for me in heaven, because I am a Jew's / daughter; and he says you are no good member of the commonwealth, for / in converting Jews to Christians you raise the price of pork.

No, you needn't worry about us, Lorenzo. Launcelet and I have fallen out. He tells me flatly there's no mercy for me in heaven because I'm a Jew's daughter, and he says you're a bad citizen, because by converting Jews to Christians you raise the price of pork.
I shall answer that better to the commonwealth than you can the getting / up of the negro's belly! The Moor is with child by you, Launcelet.
I'll answer for that to the state better than you can answer for getting the African woman pregnant! The Moorish woman is expecting your child, Launcelet.
It is much that the Moor should be more than reason; but if she be less / than an honest woman, she is indeed more than I took her for.
It's a lot for the Moor to be more than is reasonable, but if she's less than an honest woman, she's certainly more than I took her for.

How every fool can play upon the word! I think the best grace of wit / will shortly turn into silence, and discourse grow commendable in none / only but parrots. Go in, sirrah; bid them prepare for dinner.
How every fool can play with words! I think the best kind of wit will soon be silence, and talking will be admired only in parrots. Go in, sir. Tell them to get ready for dinner.
That is done, sir, they have all stomachs.
That's done, sir. They all have their appetites ready.
Goodly Lord, what a wit-snapper are you! Then bid them prepare dinner.
Good Lord, what a quick wit you are! Then tell them to get dinner ready.
That is done too, sir, only "cover" is the word.
That's done too, sir. Only "cover" is the word.
Will you lay the table, then, sir?
Not so, sir, neither. I know my duty.
No, sir, not that either. I know my place.

Yet more quarrelling with occasion! Wilt thou show the whole wealth of / thy wit in an instant? I pray thee understand a plain man in his plain / meaning: go to thy fellows, bid them cover the table, serve in the / meat, and we will come in to dinner.

Still picking a quarrel with every word! Do you want to show off all your wit at once? Please understand a plain man's plain meaning. Go to the other servants, tell them to lay the table and serve the food, and we'll come in to dinner.
For the table, sir, it shall be served in; for the meat, sir, it shall / be covered; for your coming in to dinner, sir, why, let it be as / humours and conceits shall govern.
As for the table, sir, it shall be served in. As for the food, sir, it shall be covered. As for your coming in to dinner, sir, why, let it be as your moods and fancies decide.

O dear discretion, how his words are suited! / The fool hath planted in his memory / An army of good words, and I do know / A many fools that stand in better place, / Garnish'd like him, that for a tricksy word / Defy the matter. How cheer'st thou, Jessica? / And now, good sweet, say thy opinion, / How dost thou like the Lord Bassanio's wife?

Oh, what judgment! How his words fit together! The fool has stored in his memory an army of good words, and I know many fools in higher positions, dressed up like him, who give up the sense for the sake of a clever word. How are you, Jessica? And now, my sweet, tell me what you think. How do you like Lord Bassanio's wife?

Past all expressing. It is very meet / The Lord Bassanio live an upright life, / For having such a blessing in his lady, / He finds the joys of heaven here on earth, / And if on earth he do not merit it, / In reason he should never come to heaven. / Why, if two gods should play some heavenly match, / And on the wager lay two earthly women, / And Portia one, there must be something else / Pawn'd with the other, for the poor rude world / Hath not her fellow.

More than I can say. Lord Bassanio had better live a good life, because with such a blessing in his wife he's finding the joys of heaven here on earth, and if he doesn't deserve it on earth, it stands to reason he'll never get to heaven. Why, if two gods were to make a heavenly bet and stake two earthly women on it, and Portia were one of them, something else would have to be added to the other, because this poor, rough world has no one to match her.
Even such a husband / Hast thou of me as she is for a wife.
You have just as good a husband in me as she is a wife.
Nay, but ask my opinion too of that.
No, but ask my opinion about that too.
I will anon. First let us go to dinner.
I will soon. First let's go to dinner.
Nay, let me praise you while I have a stomach.
No, let me praise you while I have an appetite for it.
No pray thee, let it serve for table-talk. / Then howsome'er thou speak'st, 'mong other things / I shall digest it.
No, please, save it for conversation at the table. Then whatever you say, I'll digest it along with everything else.
Here and ready, if it please your Grace.
I am sorry for thee, thou art come to answer / A stony adversary, an inhuman wretch, / Uncapable of pity, void and empty / From any dram of mercy.
I'm sorry for you. You've come to answer an opponent made of stone, an inhuman wretch who's incapable of pity and has not one drop of mercy in him.

I have heard / Your Grace hath ta'en great pains to qualify / His rigorous course; but since he stands obdurate, / And that no lawful means can carry me / Out of his envy's reach, I do oppose / My patience to his fury, and am arm'd / To suffer with a quietness of spirit / The very tyranny and rage of his.

I've heard that your Grace has gone to great trouble to soften his harsh course. But since he won't move, and no lawful means can carry me out of reach of his malice, I'll set my patience against his fury. I'm ready to suffer his worst tyranny and rage with a calm spirit.
Go one and call the Jew into the court.
Someone go and call the Jew into the court.
He is ready at the door. He comes, my lord.
He's waiting at the door. Here he comes, my lord.

Make room, and let him stand before our face. / Shylock, the world thinks, and I think so too, / That thou but leadest this fashion of thy malice / To the last hour of act, and then, 'tis thought, / Thou'lt show thy mercy and remorse more strange / Than is thy strange apparent cruelty; / And where thou now exacts the penalty, / Which is a pound of this poor merchant's flesh, / Thou wilt not only loose the forfeiture, / But, touch'd with human gentleness and love, / Forgive a moiety of the principal, / Glancing an eye of pity on his losses / That have of late so huddled on his back, / Enow to press a royal merchant down, / And pluck commiseration of his state / From brassy bosoms and rough hearts of flint, / From stubborn Turks and Tartars never train'd / To offices of tender courtesy. / We all expect a gentle answer, Jew.

Make room, and let him stand in front of us. Shylock, people think, and so do I, that you're only keeping up this show of malice until the last moment, and that then, people think, you'll show a mercy and pity even more surprising than your surprising cruelty seems now. And where you're now demanding the penalty, a pound of this poor merchant's flesh, you'll not only let the penalty go but, touched by human gentleness and love, forgive half of the loan, looking with pity on the losses that have piled up on his back recently, enough to crush even a great merchant, and to draw pity for his state from hearts of brass and rough hearts of flint, from stubborn Turks and Tartars never brought up to acts of kindness. We all expect a gentle answer, Jew.

I have possess'd your Grace of what I purpose, / And by our holy Sabbath have I sworn / To have the due and forfeit of my bond. / If you deny it, let the danger light / Upon your charter and your city's freedom! / You'll ask me why I rather choose to have / A weight of carrion flesh than to receive / Three thousand ducats. I'll not answer that, / But say it is my humour. Is it answer'd? / What if my house be troubled with a rat, / And I be pleas'd to give ten thousand ducats / To have it ban'd? What, are you answer'd yet? / Some men there are love not a gaping pig; / Some that are mad if they behold a cat; / And others, when the bagpipe sings i' the nose, / Cannot contain their urine; for affection / Mistress of passion, sways it to the mood / Of what it likes or loathes. Now, for your answer: / As there is no firm reason to be render'd / Why he cannot abide a gaping pig, / Why he a harmless necessary cat, / Why he a woollen bagpipe, but of force / Must yield to such inevitable shame / As to offend, himself being offended, / So can I give no reason, nor I will not, / More than a lodg'd hate and a certain loathing / I bear Antonio, that I follow thus / A losing suit against him. Are you answered?

I've told your Grace what I intend, and I've sworn by our holy Sabbath to have what's due to me under the penalty of my bond. If you deny it, let the damage fall on your city's charter and its freedom! You'll ask me why I'd rather have a weight of rotting flesh than receive three thousand ducats. I won't answer that, except to say it's my whim. Is that an answer? What if my house is troubled by a rat, and I'm happy to pay ten thousand ducats to have it poisoned? Well, is that an answer yet? Some men don't like a roast pig with its mouth open. Some go mad if they see a cat. And others, when the bagpipe plays through its nose, can't hold their water. Because instinct, which rules our feelings, steers them towards what it likes or hates. Now, for your answer. Just as there's no firm reason to give why one man can't stand an open-mouthed pig, another a harmless, useful cat, another a woollen bagpipe, but each one is forced to give in to such unavoidable shame that he gives offence because he has been offended, so I can't give any reason, and I won't, except a fixed hatred and a certain loathing I feel for Antonio, for following this losing case against him. Is that an answer?
This is no answer, thou unfeeling man, / To excuse the current of thy cruelty.
That's no answer, you unfeeling man, to excuse the course of your cruelty.
I am not bound to please thee with my answer.
I'm not obliged to please you with my answer.
Do all men kill the things they do not love?
Do all men kill the things they don't love?
Hates any man the thing he would not kill?
Does any man hate a thing he wouldn't want to kill?
Every offence is not a hate at first.
Not every offence turns to hatred straight away.
What, wouldst thou have a serpent sting thee twice?
What, would you let a snake sting you twice?
