I pray you, think you question with the Jew. / You may as well go stand upon the beach / And bid the main flood bate his usual height; / You may as well use question with the wolf, / Why he hath made the ewe bleat for the lamb; / You may as well forbid the mountain pines / To wag their high tops and to make no noise / When they are fretten with the gusts of heaven; / You may as well do anything most hard / As seek to soften that—than which what's harder?— / His Jewish heart. Therefore, I do beseech you, / Make no moe offers, use no farther means, / But with all brief and plain conveniency. / Let me have judgment, and the Jew his will.

Please, remember you're arguing with the Jew. You might as well go and stand on the beach and tell the high tide to lower its usual height. You might as well ask the wolf why he has made the ewe bleat for her lamb. You might as well forbid the mountain pines to wave their high tops and make no noise when they're shaken by the winds of heaven. You might as well do the hardest thing in the world as try to soften that, and what is harder? His Jewish heart. So, I beg you, make no more offers and try no other means, but, as quickly and simply as possible, let me have my sentence and the Jew have his will.
For thy three thousand ducats here is six.
Instead of your three thousand ducats, here are six.
If every ducat in six thousand ducats / Were in six parts, and every part a ducat, / I would not draw them, I would have my bond.
If each of the six thousand ducats were split into six parts, and every part were a ducat, I wouldn't take them. I'd have my bond.
How shalt thou hope for mercy, rend'ring none?
How can you hope for mercy if you show none?

What judgment shall I dread, doing no wrong? / You have among you many a purchas'd slave, / Which, like your asses and your dogs and mules, / You use in abject and in slavish parts, / Because you bought them. Shall I say to you / "Let them be free, marry them to your heirs? / Why sweat they under burdens? Let their beds / Be made as soft as yours, and let their palates / Be season'd with such viands"? You will answer / "The slaves are ours." So do I answer you: / The pound of flesh which I demand of him / Is dearly bought; 'tis mine and I will have it. / If you deny me, fie upon your law! / There is no force in the decrees of Venice. / I stand for judgment. Answer; shall I have it?

What judgment should I fear when I'm doing nothing wrong? You have many slaves you've bought, whom you use like your donkeys, dogs and mules for low, slavish work because you bought them. Shall I say to you, "Set them free, marry them to your children? Why are they sweating under heavy loads? Let their beds be as soft as yours, and let them eat the same food as you"? You'll answer, "The slaves are ours." So I answer you: the pound of flesh I'm demanding from him was dearly bought. It's mine, and I will have it. If you deny me, shame on your law! The laws of Venice have no force. I'm waiting for judgment. Answer: shall I have it?
Upon my power I may dismiss this court, / Unless Bellario, a learned doctor, / Whom I have sent for to determine this, / Come here today.
I have the power to adjourn this court, unless Bellario, a learned lawyer I've sent for to decide this case, arrives here today.
My lord, here stays without / A messenger with letters from the doctor, / New come from Padua.
My lord, there's a messenger waiting outside with letters from the doctor, just arrived from Padua.
Bring us the letters. Call the messenger.
Bring us the letters. Call the messenger.
Good cheer, Antonio! What, man, courage yet! / The Jew shall have my flesh, blood, bones, and all, / Ere thou shalt lose for me one drop of blood.
Cheer up, Antonio! Come on, man, take courage! The Jew will have my flesh, blood, bones and everything before you lose a single drop of blood for me.

I am a tainted wether of the flock, / Meetest for death, the weakest kind of fruit / Drops earliest to the ground, and so let me. / You cannot better be employ'd, Bassanio, / Than to live still, and write mine epitaph.
I'm the sick ram of the flock, the one best fit for death. The weakest fruit drops to the ground first, so let me. You can't do anything better, Bassanio, than go on living and write my epitaph.
Came you from Padua, from Bellario?
Have you come from Padua, from Bellario?
From both, my lord. Bellario greets your Grace.
From both, my lord. Bellario sends greetings to your Grace.
Why dost thou whet thy knife so earnestly?
Why are you sharpening your knife so keenly?
To cut the forfeiture from that bankrupt there.
To cut the penalty off that bankrupt over there.
Not on thy sole but on thy soul, harsh Jew, / Thou mak'st thy knife keen. But no metal can, / No, not the hangman's axe, bear half the keenness / Of thy sharp envy. Can no prayers pierce thee?

You're sharpening your knife not on the sole of your shoe but on your soul, harsh Jew. But no metal, not even the executioner's axe, is half as sharp as your bitter malice. Can no prayers get through to you?
No, none that thou hast wit enough to make.
No, none you're clever enough to make.

O, be thou damn'd, inexecrable dog! / And for thy life let justice be accus'd; / Thou almost mak'st me waver in my faith, / To hold opinion with Pythagoras / That souls of animals infuse themselves / Into the trunks of men. Thy currish spirit / Govern'd a wolf who, hang'd for human slaughter, / Even from the gallows did his fell soul fleet, / And whilst thou layest in thy unhallowed dam, / Infus'd itself in thee; for thy desires / Are wolfish, bloody, starv'd and ravenous.

Oh, be damned, you dog who can't be cursed enough! And let justice be blamed for letting you live. You almost make me lose my faith and agree with Pythagoras that the souls of animals pass into the bodies of men. Your currish spirit belonged to a wolf that was hanged for killing people. Its cruel soul fled straight from the gallows, while you were lying in your unholy mother's womb, and passed into you. Because your desires are wolfish, bloody, starving and greedy.
Till thou canst rail the seal from off my bond, / Thou but offend'st thy lungs to speak so loud. / Repair thy wit, good youth, or it will fall / To cureless ruin. I stand here for law.
Until you can shout the seal off my bond, you're only hurting your lungs by talking so loud. Mend your wits, good young man, or they'll fall into ruin past curing. I stand here for the law.
This letter from Bellario doth commend / A young and learned doctor to our court. / Where is he?
This letter from Bellario recommends a young and learned lawyer to our court. Where is he?
He attendeth here hard by, / To know your answer, whether you'll admit him.
He's waiting close by to hear whether you'll let him in.

With all my heart: some three or four of you / Go give him courteous conduct to this place. / Meantime, the court shall hear Bellario's letter. / [Reads] / Your Grace shall understand that at the receipt of your / letter I am very sick, but in the instant that your messenger came, in / loving visitation was with me a young doctor of Rome. His name is / Balthazar. I acquainted him with the cause in controversy between the / Jew and Antonio the merchant. We turn'd o'er many books together. He is / furnished with my opinion, which, bettered with his own learning (the / greatness whereof I cannot enough commend), comes with him at my / importunity to fill up your Grace's request in my stead. I beseech you / let his lack of years be no impediment to let him lack a reverend / estimation, for I never knew so young a body with so old a head. I / leave him to your gracious acceptance, whose trial shall better publish / his commendation. / You hear the learn'd Bellario what he writes, / And here, I take it, is the doctor come.

With all my heart. Some three or four of you, go and politely escort him here. Meanwhile, the court will hear Bellario's letter. [Reads] Your Grace should know that when your letter arrived I was very ill. But at the moment your messenger came, a young lawyer from Rome named Balthazar was paying me a friendly visit. I told him about the case in dispute between the Jew and Antonio the merchant. We looked through many books together. He has my opinion, which, improved by his own learning (which I can't praise enough), he brings with him at my request to fulfil your Grace's request in my place. Please don't let his youth stop him being respected, because I never knew such a young body with such an old head. I leave him to your kind acceptance. Testing him will show his worth better than my praise. You hear what the learned Bellario writes. And here, I think, is the lawyer.
Give me your hand. Come you from old Bellario?
Give me your hand. Have you come from old Bellario?
You are welcome. Take your place. / Are you acquainted with the difference / That holds this present question in the court?
You're welcome. Take your place. Do you know about the dispute that this court is now hearing?
I am informed throughly of the cause. / Which is the merchant here? And which the Jew?
I've been fully informed about the case. Which is the merchant here, and which is the Jew?
Antonio and old Shylock, both stand forth.
Antonio and old Shylock, both step forward.
Of a strange nature is the suit you follow, / Yet in such rule that the Venetian law / Cannot impugn you as you do proceed. / [To Antonio] You stand within his danger, do you not?
The case you're bringing is a strange one, but so properly made that Venetian law can't stop you going ahead. [To Antonio] You're in his power, aren't you?
Do you admit to the bond?
Then must the Jew be merciful.
Then the Jew must be merciful.
On what compulsion must I? Tell me that.
What forces me to? Tell me that.

The quality of mercy is not strain'd, / It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven / Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest, / It blesseth him that gives and him that takes. / 'Tis mightiest in the mightiest; it becomes / The throned monarch better than his crown. / His sceptre shows the force of temporal power, / The attribute to awe and majesty, / Wherein doth sit the dread and fear of kings; / But mercy is above this sceptred sway, / It is enthroned in the hearts of kings, / It is an attribute to God himself; / And earthly power doth then show likest God's / When mercy seasons justice. Therefore, Jew, / Though justice be thy plea, consider this, / That in the course of justice none of us / Should see salvation. We do pray for mercy, / And that same prayer doth teach us all to render / The deeds of mercy. I have spoke thus much / To mitigate the justice of thy plea, / Which if thou follow, this strict court of Venice / Must needs give sentence 'gainst the merchant there.

Mercy can't be forced. It falls like gentle rain from heaven on the ground below. It is blessed twice: it blesses the person who gives it and the person who receives it. It is mightiest in the mightiest people. It suits a king on his throne better than his crown. His sceptre shows the force of earthly power, the symbol of awe and majesty, which makes people dread and fear kings. But mercy is above the power of the sceptre. It is enthroned in the hearts of kings. It is a quality of God himself, and earthly power is most like God's when mercy softens justice. So, Jew, though justice is what you're pleading for, think about this: if we only had justice, none of us would be saved. We pray for mercy, and that same prayer teaches us all to show mercy. I've said this much to soften the justice of your claim, because if you insist on it, this strict Venetian court must give sentence against the merchant there.
My deeds upon my head! I crave the law, / The penalty and forfeit of my bond.
Let my actions be on my own head! I demand the law, the penalty and forfeit of my bond.
Is he not able to discharge the money?
Isn't he able to pay the money?

Yes, here I tender it for him in the court, / Yea, twice the sum, if that will not suffice, / I will be bound to pay it ten times o'er / On forfeit of my hands, my head, my heart. / If this will not suffice, it must appear / That malice bears down truth. And I beseech you, / Wrest once the law to your authority. / To do a great right, do a little wrong, / And curb this cruel devil of his will.

Yes, here I offer it for him in court, yes, twice the sum. If that isn't enough, I'll sign a bond to pay it ten times over, on pain of losing my hands, my head, my heart. If this isn't enough, it must be clear that malice is crushing honesty. And I beg you, bend the law just once to your authority. To do a great right, do a little wrong, and stop this cruel devil getting his way.
It must not be, there is no power in Venice / Can alter a decree established; / 'Twill be recorded for a precedent, / And many an error by the same example / Will rush into the state. It cannot be.

That can't happen. There's no power in Venice that can change an established law. It would be recorded as a precedent, and following that example many wrongs would rush into the state. It can't be done.
A Daniel come to judgment! Yea, a Daniel! / O wise young judge, how I do honour thee!
A Daniel come to judgment! Yes, a Daniel! Oh, wise young judge, how I honour you!
I pray you let me look upon the bond.
Please let me see the bond.
Here 'tis, most reverend doctor, here it is.
Here it is, most respected doctor, here it is.
Shylock, there's thrice thy money offered thee.
Shylock, you're being offered three times your money.
An oath, an oath! I have an oath in heaven. / Shall I lay perjury upon my soul? / No, not for Venice.
An oath, an oath! I've sworn an oath in heaven. Shall I put the sin of breaking it on my soul? No, not for the whole of Venice.

Why, this bond is forfeit, / And lawfully by this the Jew may claim / A pound of flesh, to be by him cut off / Nearest the merchant's heart. Be merciful, / Take thrice thy money; bid me tear the bond.
Why, this bond is forfeit, and by law the Jew can claim a pound of flesh, to be cut off by him nearest the merchant's heart. Be merciful. Take three times your money. Tell me to tear up the bond.

When it is paid according to the tenour. / It doth appear you are a worthy judge; / You know the law; your exposition / Hath been most sound. I charge you by the law, / Whereof you are a well-deserving pillar, / Proceed to judgment. By my soul I swear / There is no power in the tongue of man / To alter me. I stay here on my bond.

When it's paid according to its terms. You seem to be a worthy judge. You know the law, and your explanation has been very sound. I charge you by the law, of which you are a deserving pillar, to proceed to judgment. I swear by my soul there's no power in any man's tongue to change my mind. I stand here on my bond.
Most heartily I do beseech the court / To give the judgment.
I beg the court with all my heart to give its judgment.
Why then, thus it is: / You must prepare your bosom for his knife.
Well then, this is how it is: you must prepare your chest for his knife.
O noble judge! O excellent young man!
Oh, noble judge! Oh, excellent young man!
For the intent and purpose of the law / Hath full relation to the penalty, / Which here appeareth due upon the bond.
Because the intention and purpose of the law fully allows the penalty, which is clearly due here under the bond.
'Tis very true. O wise and upright judge, / How much more elder art thou than thy looks!
That's very true. Oh, wise and honest judge, how much older you are than you look!
Ay, his breast / So says the bond, doth it not, noble judge? / "Nearest his heart": those are the very words.
Yes, his chest. That's what the bond says, isn't it, noble judge? "Nearest his heart": those are the exact words.
It is so. Are there balance here to weigh / The flesh?
That's right. Are there scales here to weigh the flesh?
Have by some surgeon, Shylock, on your charge, / To stop his wounds, lest he do bleed to death.
Have a surgeon standing by, Shylock, at your own expense, to stop his wounds in case he bleeds to death.
Is it so nominated in the bond?
It is not so express'd, but what of that? / 'Twere good you do so much for charity.
It doesn't say so, but what of that? It would be good of you to do that much out of charity.
I cannot find it; 'tis not in the bond.
I can't find it. It isn't in the bond.
You, merchant, have you anything to say?
You, merchant, do you have anything to say?

But little. I am arm'd and well prepar'd. / Give me your hand, Bassanio. Fare you well, / Grieve not that I am fallen to this for you, / For herein Fortune shows herself more kind / Than is her custom: it is still her use / To let the wretched man outlive his wealth, / To view with hollow eye and wrinkled brow / An age of poverty, from which ling'ring penance / Of such misery doth she cut me off. / Commend me to your honourable wife, / Tell her the process of Antonio's end, / Say how I lov'd you, speak me fair in death. / And when the tale is told, bid her be judge / Whether Bassanio had not once a love. / Repent but you that you shall lose your friend / And he repents not that he pays your debt. / For if the Jew do cut but deep enough, / I'll pay it instantly with all my heart.

Very little. I'm ready and well prepared. Give me your hand, Bassanio. Goodbye. Don't grieve that this has happened to me because of you, because here Fortune is kinder than usual. Her habit is to let the wretched man outlive his wealth and face, with sunken eyes and a wrinkled forehead, an old age of poverty. She is cutting me off from that long, drawn-out punishment of misery. Give my regards to your honourable wife. Tell her how Antonio died. Say how I loved you, and speak well of me when I'm dead. And when the story is told, ask her to judge whether Bassanio was once truly loved. Only regret that you'll lose your friend, and he doesn't regret paying your debt. Because if the Jew cuts deep enough, I'll pay it at once, with all my heart.

Antonio, I am married to a wife / Which is as dear to me as life itself, / But life itself, my wife, and all the world, / Are not with me esteem'd above thy life. / I would lose all, ay, sacrifice them all / Here to this devil, to deliver you.

Antonio, I'm married to a wife who is as dear to me as life itself. But life itself, my wife and the whole world are not worth more to me than your life. I'd lose everything, yes, sacrifice it all to this devil here, to save you.
Your wife would give you little thanks for that / If she were by to hear you make the offer.
Your wife wouldn't thank you much for that, if she were here to hear you make the offer.
I have a wife who I protest I love. / I would she were in heaven, so she could / Entreat some power to change this currish Jew.
I have a wife I swear I love. I wish she were in heaven, so she could beg some power there to change this dog of a Jew.
'Tis well you offer it behind her back, / The wish would make else an unquiet house.
It's a good thing you're offering this behind her back. Otherwise that wish would make for trouble at home.
These be the Christian husbands! I have a daughter— / Would any of the stock of Barabbas / Had been her husband, rather than a Christian! / We trifle time, I pray thee, pursue sentence.
These are Christian husbands! I have a daughter. I wish any descendant of the thief Barabbas had been her husband rather than a Christian! We're wasting time. Please, get on with the sentence.
A pound of that same merchant's flesh is thine, / The court awards it and the law doth give it.
A pound of that merchant's flesh is yours. The court awards it and the law gives it.
And you must cut this flesh from off his breast. / The law allows it and the court awards it.
And you must cut this flesh from his chest. The law allows it and the court awards it.
Most learned judge! A sentence! Come, prepare.
Most learned judge! A sentence! Come, get ready.

Tarry a little, there is something else. / This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood. / The words expressly are "a pound of flesh": / Take then thy bond, take thou thy pound of flesh, / But in the cutting it, if thou dost shed / One drop of Christian blood, thy lands and goods / Are, by the laws of Venice, confiscate / Unto the state of Venice.

Wait a moment. There's something else. This bond doesn't give you a single drop of blood. The words are clearly "a pound of flesh". So take your bond, take your pound of flesh, but if, in cutting it, you shed one drop of Christian blood, your lands and goods are, by the laws of Venice, forfeit to the state of Venice.
O upright judge! Mark, Jew. O learned judge!
Oh, honest judge! Take note, Jew. Oh, learned judge!
Thyself shalt see the act. / For, as thou urgest justice, be assur'd / Thou shalt have justice more than thou desir'st.
You'll see the law yourself. Because, since you insist on justice, you can be sure you'll get more justice than you want.
O learned judge! Mark, Jew, a learned judge!
Oh, learned judge! Take note, Jew. A learned judge!
I take this offer then. Pay the bond thrice / And let the Christian go.
Then I'll take the offer. Pay the bond three times over and let the Christian go.
Soft! / The Jew shall have all justice. Soft! no haste! / He shall have nothing but the penalty.
Wait! The Jew shall have full justice. Wait! Don't hurry! He'll have nothing but the penalty.
O Jew, an upright judge, a learned judge!
Oh, Jew! An honest judge, a learned judge!

Therefore prepare thee to cut off the flesh. / Shed thou no blood, nor cut thou less nor more, / But just a pound of flesh: if thou tak'st more / Or less than a just pound, be it but so much / As makes it light or heavy in the substance, / Or the division of the twentieth part / Of one poor scruple, nay, if the scale do turn / But in the estimation of a hair, / Thou diest, and all thy goods are confiscate.

So get ready to cut off the flesh. Don't shed any blood, and don't cut less or more, but exactly a pound of flesh. If you take more or less than exactly a pound, even if it's only enough to make it lighter or heavier by a twentieth of a tiny scruple, no, if the scale tips by the weight of a single hair, you die, and all your goods are confiscated.
A second Daniel, a Daniel, Jew! / Now, infidel, I have you on the hip.
A second Daniel, a Daniel, Jew! Now, unbeliever, I've got you at my mercy.
Why doth the Jew pause? Take thy forfeiture.
Why is the Jew pausing? Take your penalty.
Give me my principal, and let me go.
Give me back my loan, and let me go.
I have it ready for thee. Here it is.
I have it ready for you. Here it is.
He hath refus'd it in the open court, / He shall have merely justice and his bond.
He refused it in open court. He'll have nothing but justice and his bond.
A Daniel still say I, a second Daniel! / I thank thee, Jew, for teaching me that word.
A Daniel, I still say, a second Daniel! Thank you, Jew, for teaching me that word.
Shall I not have barely my principal?
Can't I even have just my loan back?
Thou shalt have nothing but the forfeiture / To be so taken at thy peril, Jew.
You'll have nothing but the penalty, to be taken at your own risk, Jew.
Why, then the devil give him good of it! / I'll stay no longer question.
Why, then, may the devil give him joy of it! I won't stay to argue any longer.

Tarry, Jew. / The law hath yet another hold on you. / It is enacted in the laws of Venice, / If it be proved against an alien / That by direct or indirect attempts / He seek the life of any citizen, / The party 'gainst the which he doth contrive / Shall seize one half his goods; the other half / Comes to the privy coffer of the state, / And the offender's life lies in the mercy / Of the Duke only, 'gainst all other voice. / In which predicament I say thou stand'st; / For it appears by manifest proceeding / That indirectly, and directly too, / Thou hast contrived against the very life / Of the defendant; and thou hast incurr'd / The danger formerly by me rehears'd. / Down, therefore, and beg mercy of the Duke.

Wait, Jew. The law has another hold on you. The laws of Venice say that if it's proved against a foreigner that he has tried, directly or indirectly, to take the life of any citizen, the person he plotted against shall take half his goods. The other half goes to the state treasury, and the offender's life lies at the mercy of the Duke alone, whatever anyone else says. That's the position I say you're in, because it's clear from what has happened here that you have plotted, indirectly and directly too, against the defendant's very life, and you've incurred the penalty I've just described. So get down on your knees and beg the Duke for mercy.
Beg that thou mayst have leave to hang thyself, / And yet, thy wealth being forfeit to the state, / Thou hast not left the value of a cord; / Therefore thou must be hang'd at the state's charge.
Beg for permission to hang yourself. And yet, since your wealth is forfeit to the state, you haven't got enough left to buy a rope. So you'll have to be hanged at the state's expense.

That thou shalt see the difference of our spirit, / I pardon thee thy life before thou ask it. / For half thy wealth, it is Antonio's; / The other half comes to the general state, / Which humbleness may drive unto a fine.

So that you can see how different our spirit is, I pardon your life before you ask for it. As for half your wealth, it belongs to Antonio. The other half goes to the state, though if you show humility that may be reduced to a fine.
Ay, for the state, not for Antonio.
Yes, for the state's half, not for Antonio's.
Nay, take my life and all, pardon not that. / You take my house when you do take the prop / That doth sustain my house; you take my life / When you do take the means whereby I live.
No, take my life and everything. Don't pardon that. You take my house when you take the prop that holds my house up. You take my life when you take the means I live by.
What mercy can you render him, Antonio?
What mercy can you show him, Antonio?
A halter gratis, nothing else, for God's sake!
A free noose, nothing else, for God's sake!

So please my lord the Duke and all the court / To quit the fine for one half of his goods, / I am content, so he will let me have / The other half in use, to render it / Upon his death unto the gentleman / That lately stole his daughter. / Two things provided more, that for this favour, / He presently become a Christian; / The other, that he do record a gift, / Here in the court, of all he dies possess'd / Unto his son Lorenzo and his daughter.

If my lord the Duke and all the court will let him off the fine for the state's half of his goods, I'm satisfied, as long as he lets me have the other half in trust, to hand over when he dies to the gentleman who recently ran off with his daughter. Two more conditions: first, in return for this favour, he must become a Christian at once. Second, he must sign a deed here in court leaving everything he owns when he dies to his son-in-law Lorenzo and his daughter.
He shall do this, or else I do recant / The pardon that I late pronounced here.
He'll do this, or else I take back the pardon I've just given here.
Art thou contented, Jew? What dost thou say?
Are you satisfied, Jew? What do you say?
Clerk, draw a deed of gift.
Clerk, draw up a deed of gift.
I pray you give me leave to go from hence; / I am not well; send the deed after me / And I will sign it.
Please give me permission to leave. I'm not well. Send the deed after me and I'll sign it.
Get thee gone, but do it.
In christ'ning shalt thou have two god-fathers. / Had I been judge, thou shouldst have had ten more, / To bring thee to the gallows, not to the font.
At your christening you'll have two godfathers. If I'd been the judge, you'd have had ten more, a jury, to bring you to the gallows, not to the font.
Sir, I entreat you home with me to dinner.
Sir, please come home with me to dinner.
I humbly do desire your Grace of pardon, / I must away this night toward Padua, / And it is meet I presently set forth.
I humbly beg your Grace's pardon. I must leave for Padua tonight, and I ought to set off at once.
I am sorry that your leisure serves you not. / Antonio, gratify this gentleman, / For in my mind you are much bound to him.
I'm sorry you haven't the time. Antonio, reward this gentleman, because in my opinion you owe him a great deal.

Most worthy gentleman, I and my friend / Have by your wisdom been this day acquitted / Of grievous penalties, in lieu whereof, / Three thousand ducats due unto the Jew / We freely cope your courteous pains withal.

Most worthy gentleman, thanks to your wisdom my friend and I have today been freed from terrible penalties. In return, we gladly give you the three thousand ducats that were owed to the Jew, for your kind trouble.
And stand indebted, over and above / In love and service to you evermore.
And we remain in your debt, over and above that, with love and service for ever.

He is well paid that is well satisfied, / And I delivering you, am satisfied, / And therein do account myself well paid, / My mind was never yet more mercenary. / I pray you know me when we meet again, / I wish you well, and so I take my leave.

A man who is well satisfied is well paid, and I, by saving you, am satisfied, and so I count myself well paid. My mind was never more interested in money than that. Please recognise me when we meet again. I wish you well, and so I'll say goodbye.
Dear sir, of force I must attempt you further. / Take some remembrance of us as a tribute, / Not as fee. Grant me two things, I pray you, / Not to deny me, and to pardon me.
Dear sir, I really must press you further. Take some keepsake from us as a token, not as a fee. Please grant me two things: don't refuse me, and forgive me for insisting.

You press me far, and therefore I will yield. / [To Antonio] Give me your gloves, I'll wear them for your sake. / [To Bassanio] And, for your love, I'll take this ring from you. / Do not draw back your hand; I'll take no more, / And you in love shall not deny me this.

You press me hard, so I'll give in. [To Antonio] Give me your gloves. I'll wear them for your sake. [To Bassanio] And, for your love, I'll take this ring from you. Don't pull your hand back. I won't take anything else, and out of love you won't refuse me this.
This ring, good sir? Alas, it is a trifle, / I will not shame myself to give you this.
This ring, good sir? Oh, it's just a trifle. I won't shame myself by giving you this.
I will have nothing else but only this, / And now methinks I have a mind to it.
I'll have nothing else but this, and now I think I've set my heart on it.
There's more depends on this than on the value. / The dearest ring in Venice will I give you, / And find it out by proclamation, / Only for this I pray you pardon me.
There's more to this than what it's worth. I'll give you the most valuable ring in Venice, and find it by public announcement. Only, please excuse me from giving you this one.
I see, sir, you are liberal in offers. / You taught me first to beg, and now methinks / You teach me how a beggar should be answer'd.
I see, sir, you're generous with offers. First you taught me to beg, and now, it seems, you're teaching me how a beggar should be answered.
Good sir, this ring was given me by my wife, / And when she put it on, she made me vow / That I should neither sell, nor give, nor lose it.
Good sir, my wife gave me this ring, and when she put it on she made me swear I'd never sell it, give it away or lose it.

That 'scuse serves many men to save their gifts. / And if your wife be not a mad-woman, / And know how well I have deserv'd this ring, / She would not hold out enemy for ever / For giving it to me. Well, peace be with you!

That excuse helps many men keep their gifts. And unless your wife is a madwoman, if she knew how well I'd earned this ring, she wouldn't stay angry with you for ever for giving it to me. Well, peace be with you!
My Lord Bassanio, let him have the ring. / Let his deservings and my love withal / Be valued 'gainst your wife's commandment.
My Lord Bassanio, let him have the ring. Let what he deserves, and my love as well, count for more than your wife's command.
Go, Gratiano, run and overtake him; / Give him the ring, and bring him if thou canst / Unto Antonio's house. Away, make haste.
Go, Gratiano, run and catch him up. Give him the ring, and bring him to Antonio's house if you can. Go, hurry.
Come, you and I will thither presently, / And in the morning early will we both / Fly toward Belmont. Come, Antonio.
Come, you and I will go there at once, and early in the morning we'll both hurry to Belmont. Come, Antonio.
Inquire the Jew's house out, give him this deed, / And let him sign it, we'll away tonight, / And be a day before our husbands home. / This deed will be well welcome to Lorenzo.
Find out where the Jew lives, give him this deed and get him to sign it. We'll leave tonight and be home a day before our husbands. Lorenzo will be very glad of this deed.
Fair sir, you are well o'erta'en. / My Lord Bassanio upon more advice, / Hath sent you here this ring, and doth entreat / Your company at dinner.
Fair sir, I'm glad I've caught you. My Lord Bassanio, having thought it over, has sent you this ring, and asks you to have dinner with him.
That cannot be; / His ring I do accept most thankfully, / And so I pray you tell him. Furthermore, / I pray you show my youth old Shylock's house.
That's not possible. I accept his ring most gratefully, and please tell him so. And please show my young clerk old Shylock's house.
Sir, I would speak with you. / [Aside to Portia] / I'll see if I can get my husband's ring, / Which I did make him swear to keep for ever.
Sir, I'd like a word with you. [Aside to Portia] I'll see if I can get my husband's ring, which I made him swear to keep for ever.

[To Nerissa] Thou mayst, I warrant. We shall have old swearing / That they did give the rings away to men; / But we'll outface them, and outswear them too. / Away! make haste! Thou know'st where I will tarry.
[To Nerissa] You can, I'm sure. We'll hear plenty of swearing that they gave the rings away to men. But we'll stare them down and outswear them too. Go, hurry! You know where I'll wait.
Come, good sir, will you show me to this house?
Come, good sir, will you show me this house?

The moon shines bright. In such a night as this, / When the sweet wind did gently kiss the trees, / And they did make no noise, in such a night, / Troilus methinks mounted the Trojan walls, / And sigh'd his soul toward the Grecian tents / Where Cressid lay that night.

The moon is shining brightly. On a night like this, when the sweet wind was gently kissing the trees and they made no sound, on a night like this, I think, Troilus climbed the walls of Troy and sighed out his soul towards the Greek tents where Cressida lay that night.
In such a night / Did Thisbe fearfully o'ertrip the dew, / And saw the lion's shadow ere himself, / And ran dismay'd away.
On a night like this Thisbe tripped fearfully over the dew, saw the lion's shadow before she saw the lion itself, and ran away in terror.
In such a night / Stood Dido with a willow in her hand / Upon the wild sea-banks, and waft her love / To come again to Carthage.
On a night like this Dido stood on the wild seashore with a willow branch in her hand, waving to her lover to come back to Carthage.
In such a night / Medea gathered the enchanted herbs / That did renew old Æson.
On a night like this Medea gathered the magic herbs that made old Aeson young again.
In such a night / Did Jessica steal from the wealthy Jew, / And with an unthrift love did run from Venice / As far as Belmont.
On a night like this Jessica stole away from the rich Jew, and ran from Venice with a penniless lover all the way to Belmont.
In such a night / Did young Lorenzo swear he loved her well, / Stealing her soul with many vows of faith, / And ne'er a true one.
On a night like this young Lorenzo swore he loved her truly, stealing her soul with many vows of faithfulness, and not one of them true.
In such a night / Did pretty Jessica, like a little shrew, / Slander her love, and he forgave it her.
On a night like this pretty Jessica, like a little scold, slandered her lover, and he forgave her.
I would out-night you did no body come; / But hark, I hear the footing of a man.
I'd beat you at this "night" game if nobody came. But listen, I can hear a man's footsteps.
Who comes so fast in silence of the night?
Who's coming so fast in the silence of the night?
A friend! What friend? Your name, I pray you, friend?
A friend! What friend? Your name, please, friend?
Stephano is my name, and I bring word / My mistress will before the break of day / Be here at Belmont. She doth stray about / By holy crosses where she kneels and prays / For happy wedlock hours.
Stephano is my name, and I've come to tell you my mistress will be here at Belmont before daybreak. She's travelling around the holy wayside crosses, where she kneels and prays for a happy marriage.
None but a holy hermit and her maid. / I pray you is my master yet return'd?
Nobody but a holy hermit and her maid. Please, has my master come back yet?
He is not, nor we have not heard from him. / But go we in, I pray thee, Jessica, / And ceremoniously let us prepare / Some welcome for the mistress of the house.
He hasn't, and we haven't heard from him. But let's go in, please, Jessica, and prepare a proper ceremonial welcome for the mistress of the house.
Sola, sola! wo ha, ho! sola, sola!
Sola, sola! Whoa, ho! Sola, sola!
Sola! Did you see Master Lorenzo? Master Lorenzo! Sola, sola!
Sola! Have you seen Master Lorenzo? Master Lorenzo! Sola, sola!
Tell him there's a post come from my master with his horn full of good / news. My master will be here ere morning.
Tell him a messenger has come from my master with his horn full of good news. My master will be here before morning.

Sweet soul, let's in, and there expect their coming. / And yet no matter; why should we go in? / My friend Stephano, signify, I pray you, / Within the house, your mistress is at hand, / And bring your music forth into the air.

Sweet soul, let's go in and wait for them to arrive there. And yet, never mind, why should we go in? My friend Stephano, please announce inside the house that your mistress is close by, and bring the musicians out into the open air.

How sweet the moonlight sleeps upon this bank! / Here will we sit and let the sounds of music / Creep in our ears; soft stillness and the night / Become the touches of sweet harmony. / Sit, Jessica. Look how the floor of heaven / Is thick inlaid with patens of bright gold. / There's not the smallest orb which thou behold'st / But in his motion like an angel sings, / Still quiring to the young-eyed cherubins; / Such harmony is in immortal souls, / But whilst this muddy vesture of decay / Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it.

How sweetly the moonlight sleeps on this bank! We'll sit here and let the sounds of music creep into our ears. Soft stillness and the night suit the notes of sweet harmony. Sit, Jessica. Look how the floor of heaven is thickly inlaid with discs of bright gold. There isn't a single star you can see, not even the smallest, that doesn't sing like an angel as it moves, always singing in harmony with the bright-eyed cherubs. Immortal souls have that kind of harmony in them, but while our souls are shut inside these coarse, muddy bodies that decay, we can't hear it.
Come, ho! and wake Diana with a hymn. / With sweetest touches pierce your mistress' ear, / And draw her home with music.
Come on! Wake the moon goddess with a hymn. Reach your mistress's ear with your sweetest playing, and draw her home with music.
I am never merry when I hear sweet music.
Sweet music never makes me merry.

The reason is, your spirits are attentive. / For do but note a wild and wanton herd / Or race of youthful and unhandled colts, / Fetching mad bounds, bellowing and neighing loud, / Which is the hot condition of their blood, / If they but hear perchance a trumpet sound, / Or any air of music touch their ears, / You shall perceive them make a mutual stand, / Their savage eyes turn'd to a modest gaze / By the sweet power of music: therefore the poet / Did feign that Orpheus drew trees, stones, and floods, / Since naught so stockish, hard, and full of rage, / But music for the time doth change his nature. / The man that hath no music in himself, / Nor is not mov'd with concord of sweet sounds, / Is fit for treasons, stratagems, and spoils; / The motions of his spirit are dull as night, / And his affections dark as Erebus. / Let no such man be trusted. Mark the music.

The reason is that your spirits are paying attention. Just look at a wild, frisky herd, or a group of young, untamed colts, leaping madly about, bellowing and neighing loudly, as their hot blood makes them do. If they happen to hear a trumpet, or any tune reaches their ears, you'll see them all stand still together, their wild eyes turned to a gentle gaze by the sweet power of music. That's why the poet invented the story that Orpheus could make trees, stones and rivers follow him, because nothing is so dull, hard and full of rage that music can't change its nature for a while. The man who has no music in him, and isn't moved by the harmony of sweet sounds, is fit for treason, plots and robbery. The workings of his spirit are as dull as night, and his feelings as dark as hell. Don't trust a man like that. Listen to the music.
That light we see is burning in my hall. / How far that little candle throws his beams! / So shines a good deed in a naughty world.
That light we can see is burning in my hall. How far that little candle throws its beams! That's how a good deed shines in a wicked world.
When the moon shone we did not see the candle.
When the moon was shining we didn't see the candle.

So doth the greater glory dim the less. / A substitute shines brightly as a king / Until a king be by, and then his state / Empties itself, as doth an inland brook / Into the main of waters. Music! hark!
That's how the greater glory dims the lesser. A deputy shines as brightly as a king until a king is near, and then his greatness drains away, like a stream flowing into the sea. Music! Listen!
It is your music, madam, of the house.
It's your own musicians from the house, madam.
Nothing is good, I see, without respect. / Methinks it sounds much sweeter than by day.
Nothing is good, I see, except in its setting. I think it sounds much sweeter than by day.
Silence bestows that virtue on it, madam.
Silence gives it that quality, madam.

The crow doth sing as sweetly as the lark / When neither is attended; and I think / The nightingale, if she should sing by day / When every goose is cackling, would be thought / No better a musician than the wren. / How many things by season season'd are / To their right praise and true perfection! / Peace! How the moon sleeps with Endymion, / And would not be awak'd!

The crow sings as sweetly as the lark when nobody is listening. And I think if the nightingale sang by day, when every goose is cackling, she'd be thought no better a musician than the wren. How many things are made perfect, and win their proper praise, by coming at the right time! Quiet! The moon is sleeping with Endymion and doesn't want to be woken.
That is the voice, / Or I am much deceiv'd, of Portia.
That's Portia's voice, unless I'm very much mistaken.
He knows me as the blind man knows the cuckoo, / By the bad voice.
He knows me the way a blind man knows the cuckoo, by its bad voice.
We have been praying for our husbands' welfare, / Which speed, we hope, the better for our words. / Are they return'd?
We've been praying for our husbands' wellbeing, and we hope they're doing better for our prayers. Have they come back?
Madam, they are not yet; / But there is come a messenger before / To signify their coming.
Not yet, madam. But a messenger has come ahead to announce that they're coming.
Go in, Nerissa. / Give order to my servants, that they take / No note at all of our being absent hence, / Nor you, Lorenzo; Jessica, nor you.
Go in, Nerissa. Tell my servants not to say a word about our being away. And you too, Lorenzo, and you, Jessica.
Your husband is at hand, I hear his trumpet. / We are no tell-tales, madam, fear you not.
Your husband is close by. I can hear his trumpet. We're no tell-tales, madam, don't worry.
This night methinks is but the daylight sick, / It looks a little paler. 'Tis a day / Such as the day is when the sun is hid.
I think this night is just a sickly daylight. It looks a little paler. It's a day like a day when the sun is hidden.
We should hold day with the Antipodes, / If you would walk in absence of the sun.
We'd have daylight at the same time as people on the other side of the world if you walked about when the sun was gone.
Let me give light, but let me not be light, / For a light wife doth make a heavy husband, / And never be Bassanio so for me. / But God sort all! You are welcome home, my lord.

Let me give light, but don't let me be light, because an unfaithful wife makes her husband heavy-hearted, and I'd never want Bassanio to be like that because of me. But God decides everything! Welcome home, my lord.
I thank you, madam. Give welcome to my friend. / This is the man, this is Antonio, / To whom I am so infinitely bound.
Thank you, madam. Welcome my friend. This is the man, this is Antonio, to whom I owe so much.
You should in all sense be much bound to him, / For, as I hear, he was much bound for you.
You should be bound to him in every sense, because, as I hear, he was put in bonds for you.
No more than I am well acquitted of.
No more than I've been well freed from.
Sir, you are very welcome to our house. / It must appear in other ways than words, / Therefore I scant this breathing courtesy.
Sir, you're very welcome to our house. It must be shown in other ways than words, so I'll cut short this spoken politeness.
[To Nerissa] By yonder moon I swear you do me wrong, / In faith, I gave it to the judge's clerk. / Would he were gelt that had it, for my part, / Since you do take it, love, so much at heart.

[To Nerissa] I swear by that moon you're wronging me. Honestly, I gave it to the judge's clerk. As far as I'm concerned, I wish the man who has it were castrated, since you take it so much to heart, love.
A quarrel, ho, already! What's the matter?
What, a quarrel already! What's the matter?
About a hoop of gold, a paltry ring / That she did give me, whose posy was / For all the world like cutlers' poetry / Upon a knife, "Love me, and leave me not."
It's about a hoop of gold, a worthless ring she gave me, with a motto exactly like the poetry cutlers engrave on knives: "Love me, and leave me not."

What talk you of the posy, or the value? / You swore to me when I did give it you, / That you would wear it till your hour of death, / And that it should lie with you in your grave. / Though not for me, yet for your vehement oaths, / You should have been respective and have kept it. / Gave it a judge's clerk! No, God's my judge, / The clerk will ne'er wear hair on's face that had it.

Why are you talking about the motto, or the value? You swore to me when I gave it to you that you'd wear it until you died, and that it would lie with you in your grave. If not for my sake, then for the sake of your passionate oaths, you should have respected it and kept it. Gave it to a judge's clerk! No, God is my judge, the clerk who has it will never grow hair on his face.
He will, and if he live to be a man.
He will, if he lives to be a man.
Ay, if a woman live to be a man.
Yes, if a woman lives to be a man.

Now, by this hand, I gave it to a youth, / A kind of boy, a little scrubbed boy, / No higher than thyself, the judge's clerk, / A prating boy that begg'd it as a fee, / I could not for my heart deny it him.

Now, I swear by this hand, I gave it to a youth, a sort of boy, a scrubby little boy no taller than you, the judge's clerk. A chattering boy who begged for it as his fee. I couldn't for the life of me refuse him.

You were to blame,—I must be plain with you,— / To part so slightly with your wife's first gift, / A thing stuck on with oaths upon your finger, / And so riveted with faith unto your flesh. / I gave my love a ring, and made him swear / Never to part with it, and here he stands. / I dare be sworn for him he would not leave it / Nor pluck it from his finger for the wealth / That the world masters. Now, in faith, Gratiano, / You give your wife too unkind a cause of grief, / An 'twere to me I should be mad at it.

You were to blame, I have to be honest with you, to part so lightly with your wife's first gift, a thing fixed on your finger with oaths and riveted to your flesh by your promise. I gave my love a ring and made him swear never to part with it, and here he stands. I'd swear for him that he wouldn't give it away or pull it off his finger for all the wealth in the world. Now, honestly, Gratiano, you're giving your wife too cruel a reason to be upset. If it were me, I'd be furious.
[Aside] Why, I were best to cut my left hand off, / And swear I lost the ring defending it.
[Aside] Why, I'd better cut my left hand off and swear I lost the ring defending it.

My Lord Bassanio gave his ring away / Unto the judge that begg'd it, and indeed / Deserv'd it too. And then the boy, his clerk, / That took some pains in writing, he begg'd mine, / And neither man nor master would take aught / But the two rings.

My Lord Bassanio gave his ring away to the judge who begged for it, and who did deserve it too. And then the boy, his clerk, who had taken some trouble writing, begged for mine. And neither the man nor his master would take anything except the two rings.
What ring gave you, my lord? / Not that, I hope, which you receiv'd of me.
Which ring did you give, my lord? Not the one I gave you, I hope.
If I could add a lie unto a fault, / I would deny it, but you see my finger / Hath not the ring upon it, it is gone.
If I could add a lie to my fault, I'd deny it. But you can see my finger hasn't got the ring on it. It's gone.
Even so void is your false heart of truth. / By heaven, I will ne'er come in your bed / Until I see the ring.
Your false heart is just as empty of truth. By heaven, I'll never come into your bed until I see the ring.
Nor I in yours / Till I again see mine!
And I won't come into yours until I see mine again!

Sweet Portia, / If you did know to whom I gave the ring, / If you did know for whom I gave the ring, / And would conceive for what I gave the ring, / And how unwillingly I left the ring, / When nought would be accepted but the ring, / You would abate the strength of your displeasure.

Sweet Portia, if you knew who I gave the ring to, if you knew for whose sake I gave the ring, and could understand what I gave the ring for, and how unwillingly I let go of the ring, when nothing would be accepted but the ring, you'd soften your anger.

If you had known the virtue of the ring, / Or half her worthiness that gave the ring, / Or your own honour to contain the ring, / You would not then have parted with the ring. / What man is there so much unreasonable, / If you had pleas'd to have defended it / With any terms of zeal, wanted the modesty / To urge the thing held as a ceremony? / Nerissa teaches me what to believe: / I'll die for't but some woman had the ring.

If you had known the power of the ring, or half the worth of the woman who gave you the ring, or how your own honour depended on keeping the ring, you wouldn't have parted with the ring. What man would be so unreasonable, if you'd cared to defend it with any passion at all, that he'd be rude enough to insist on taking something kept as a sacred token? Nerissa is teaching me what to believe. I'd bet my life some woman got the ring.

No, by my honour, madam, by my soul, / No woman had it, but a civil doctor, / Which did refuse three thousand ducats of me, / And begg'd the ring, the which I did deny him, / And suffer'd him to go displeas'd away, / Even he that had held up the very life / Of my dear friend. What should I say, sweet lady? / I was enforc'd to send it after him. / I was beset with shame and courtesy. / My honour would not let ingratitude / So much besmear it. Pardon me, good lady; / For by these blessed candles of the night, / Had you been there, I think you would have begg'd / The ring of me to give the worthy doctor.

No, on my honour, madam, by my soul, no woman got it, but a doctor of law, who refused three thousand ducats from me and begged for the ring. I refused him, and let him go away offended, the very man who had saved the life of my dear friend. What could I do, sweet lady? I was forced to send it after him. I was overcome by shame and the need to be polite. My honour wouldn't let ingratitude smear it so badly. Forgive me, good lady, because by these blessed candles of the night, the stars, I think if you'd been there you would have begged me for the ring to give to the worthy doctor.

Let not that doctor e'er come near my house, / Since he hath got the jewel that I loved, / And that which you did swear to keep for me, / I will become as liberal as you, / I'll not deny him anything I have, / No, not my body, nor my husband's bed. / Know him I shall, I am well sure of it. / Lie not a night from home. Watch me like Argus, / If you do not, if I be left alone, / Now by mine honour which is yet mine own, / I'll have that doctor for mine bedfellow.

Never let that doctor come near my house. Since he has the jewel I loved, the one you swore to keep for me, I'll be as generous as you. I won't refuse him anything I have, no, not my body, nor my husband's bed. I'll get to know him, I'm quite sure of it. Don't spend a single night away from home. Watch me like hundred-eyed Argus. If you don't, if I'm left alone, then, by my honour, which is still my own, I'll have that doctor for my bedfellow.
And I his clerk. Therefore be well advis'd / How you do leave me to mine own protection.
And I'll have his clerk. So think carefully before you leave me to look after myself.
Well, do you so. Let not me take him then, / For if I do, I'll mar the young clerk's pen.
Well, do that. But don't let me catch him then, because if I do, I'll spoil the young clerk's pen.
I am th' unhappy subject of these quarrels.
I'm the unhappy cause of these quarrels.
Sir, grieve not you. You are welcome notwithstanding.
Sir, don't be upset. You're welcome all the same.
Portia, forgive me this enforced wrong, / And in the hearing of these many friends / I swear to thee, even by thine own fair eyes, / Wherein I see myself—
Portia, forgive me this wrong I was forced into, and in front of all these friends I swear to you, even by your own beautiful eyes, in which I see myself—
Mark you but that! / In both my eyes he doubly sees himself, / In each eye one. Swear by your double self, / And there's an oath of credit.
Just listen to that! He sees himself twice, in both my eyes, one in each. Swear by your double self, your two-faced self, and that's an oath to trust.
Nay, but hear me. / Pardon this fault, and by my soul I swear / I never more will break an oath with thee.
No, but listen to me. Forgive this fault, and I swear by my soul I'll never break a promise to you again.

I once did lend my body for his wealth, / Which but for him that had your husband's ring / Had quite miscarried. I dare be bound again, / My soul upon the forfeit, that your lord / Will never more break faith advisedly.

I once lent my body for his sake, and it would have been lost completely if it hadn't been for the man who has your husband's ring. I dare to sign a bond again, with my soul as the penalty, that your husband will never knowingly break faith again.
Then you shall be his surety. Give him this, / And bid him keep it better than the other.
Then you'll be his guarantor. Give him this, and tell him to keep it better than the other one.
Here, Lord Bassanio, swear to keep this ring.
Here, Lord Bassanio, swear to keep this ring.
By heaven, it is the same I gave the doctor!
By heaven, it's the same one I gave the doctor!
I had it of him: pardon me, Bassanio, / For by this ring, the doctor lay with me.
I got it from him. Forgive me, Bassanio, because for this ring the doctor slept with me.
And pardon me, my gentle Gratiano, / For that same scrubbed boy, the doctor's clerk, / In lieu of this, last night did lie with me.
And forgive me, my gentle Gratiano, because that same scrubby boy, the doctor's clerk, slept with me last night in return for this.
Why, this is like the mending of highways / In summer, where the ways are fair enough. / What, are we cuckolds ere we have deserv'd it?
Why, this is like repairing the roads in summer, when they're good enough already. What, are we cuckolds before we've deserved it?

Speak not so grossly. You are all amaz'd. / Here is a letter; read it at your leisure. / It comes from Padua from Bellario. / There you shall find that Portia was the doctor, / Nerissa there, her clerk. Lorenzo here / Shall witness I set forth as soon as you, / And even but now return'd. I have not yet / Enter'd my house. Antonio, you are welcome, / And I have better news in store for you / Than you expect: unseal this letter soon. / There you shall find three of your argosies / Are richly come to harbour suddenly. / You shall not know by what strange accident / I chanced on this letter.

Don't talk so crudely. You're all bewildered. Here's a letter. Read it when you have time. It comes from Bellario in Padua. In it you'll find that Portia was the doctor and Nerissa there her clerk. Lorenzo here will swear that I left as soon as you did and have only just come back. I haven't even been into my house yet. Antonio, you're welcome, and I have better news for you than you expect. Open this letter quickly. In it you'll find that three of your merchant ships have suddenly arrived in harbour, richly loaded. You won't find out by what strange chance I came across this letter.
Were you the doctor, and I knew you not?
Were you the doctor, and I didn't recognise you?
Were you the clerk that is to make me cuckold?
Were you the clerk who's going to make me a cuckold?
Ay, but the clerk that never means to do it, / Unless he live until he be a man.
Yes, but the clerk who never means to do it, unless he lives to become a man.
Sweet doctor, you shall be my bedfellow. / When I am absent, then lie with my wife.
Sweet doctor, you'll be my bedfellow. When I'm away, sleep with my wife then.
Sweet lady, you have given me life and living; / For here I read for certain that my ships / Are safely come to road.
Sweet lady, you've given me my life and my living, because here I read for certain that my ships have come safely into harbour.
How now, Lorenzo! / My clerk hath some good comforts too for you.
How are you, Lorenzo! My clerk has some good comfort for you too.
Ay, and I'll give them him without a fee. / There do I give to you and Jessica, / From the rich Jew, a special deed of gift, / After his death, of all he dies possess'd of.
Yes, and I'll give it to him without charging a fee. Here I give to you and Jessica a special deed of gift from the rich Jew, leaving you everything he owns when he dies.
Fair ladies, you drop manna in the way / Of starved people.
Beautiful ladies, you're dropping heavenly food in the path of starving people.
It is almost morning, / And yet I am sure you are not satisfied / Of these events at full. Let us go in, / And charge us there upon inter'gatories, / And we will answer all things faithfully.
It's almost morning, and yet I'm sure you aren't fully satisfied about what happened. Let's go in, and you can question us there under oath, and we'll answer everything truthfully.

Let it be so. The first inter'gatory / That my Nerissa shall be sworn on is, / Whether till the next night she had rather stay, / Or go to bed now, being two hours to day. / But were the day come, I should wish it dark / Till I were couching with the doctor's clerk. / Well, while I live, I'll fear no other thing / So sore as keeping safe Nerissa's ring.

Let's do that. The first question my Nerissa will have to answer on oath is whether she'd rather wait until tomorrow night or go to bed now, with two hours to go before daylight. But if it were day already, I'd wish it were dark, so I could be in bed with the doctor's clerk. Well, as long as I live, I'll worry about nothing so much as keeping Nerissa's ring safe.
